Investments Landscape.overview: This chapter sets the scene for alternative investing. It explains how investment differs from saving and speculation, the difference between real and financial assets, nominal versus real returns, and how traditional assets (listed equity, bonds, cash) compare with alternatives such as hedge-fund style strategies, private equity and real estate. Learners should be clear on the typical features of alternatives — lower liquidity, higher fees, less transparency and complex valuation — and on investor concepts like risk tolerance, risk capacity, time horizon and the idea of absolute versus relative return mandates. Revise the definitions carefully, because later chapters build on them.
questions: Which of the following is a real asset rather than a financial asset?
A listed corporate bond of a logistics company
Units of a liquid mutual fund scheme
A fixed deposit receipt issued by a scheduled bank
A warehouse leased out to a logistics company

A real asset is a physical or tangible asset that produces value directly, such as property, land or machinery. Bonds, mutual fund units and deposits are financial claims on someone else's assets or cash flows.
Compared with long-only listed equity funds, alternative investment strategies typically show:
Daily liquidity, lower fees and fully standardised valuation
Guaranteed returns with complete transparency of every position
Lower minimum ticket sizes aimed at small retail savers
Lower liquidity, higher fees and more complex valuation

Alternatives usually carry lock-ins or redemption limits, management plus performance fees and positions that are harder to value. They are meant for sophisticated investors, not small savers, and returns are never guaranteed.
A portfolio earned a nominal return of 12% in a year when inflation was 5%. Its real return, computed exactly, is closest to:
Real return = (1 + nominal) / (1 + inflation) − 1 = 1.12 / 1.05 − 1 = 6.67%. Simply subtracting 5 from 12 gives 7%, which is only an approximation that overstates the real return.
A Category III fund states that its objective is to deliver positive returns in both rising and falling markets. This is best described as:
An absolute return mandate
A relative return mandate measured only against the Nifty 50
A passive index-replication mandate with low tracking error
A capital protection mandate backed by a bank guarantee

An absolute return mandate targets positive returns regardless of market direction, often using shorting and hedging. A relative return mandate only seeks to beat a benchmark, even if the benchmark itself falls.
The hedge fund structure is commonly traced back to Alfred Winslow Jones, whose fund combined:
Only government bonds held to maturity
Commodity futures and physical gold storage
Long stock positions, short sales and leverage
Real estate rental income and infrastructure loans
Jones bought stocks he liked, shorted stocks he disliked to reduce market exposure, and used leverage to magnify stock-picking returns. This 'hedged' long-short idea gave hedge funds their name.
An investor needs a large part of her portfolio to pay for her daughter's overseas education in 18 months. Which constraint should dominate any decision to invest in a Category III AIF?
Her preference for funds with famous managers
The fund's past three-year return compared with peers
Liquidity needs and the short time horizon
Whether the fund invests mainly in large-cap stocks

Money needed within 18 months should not be locked in vehicles with lock-ins, gates or volatile returns. Liquidity and horizon are binding constraints; past returns or manager reputation cannot override them.
Why do investors generally demand a 'liquidity premium' from alternative investments?
Because SEBI mandates a minimum return for all alternative funds
Because liquid investments are always taxed at higher rates in India
They accept that money may be hard to withdraw quickly at fair value
Because illiquid assets have no price volatility at all

When capital can be locked in or sold only at a discount, investors expect extra return as compensation. No regulation guarantees AIF returns, and illiquid assets still carry risk even if prices are observed less often.
Under SEBI's accredited investor framework, accreditation certificates are issued by:
The AIF manager after reviewing the investor's bank statements
The Income Tax Department through the annual tax return
Accreditation agencies recognised for this purpose by SEBI
Any registered stock broker with whom the investor trades

SEBI designates accreditation agencies (subsidiaries of depositories and exchanges) to verify income or net worth and issue accreditation. A fund manager cannot self-certify an investor as accredited.

Types of Investments.overview: This chapter introduces the instruments a Category III manager can use: listed equity, debt and money-market instruments, futures, options, swaps and structured exposures, as well as cash-equivalents used as collateral. Focus on how each instrument changes the fund's exposure — for example, how futures give leveraged exposure for a small margin, how short positions profit from falling prices, and how option buyers and sellers face very different risk profiles. Practise simple pay-off calculations for futures and options, and understand why derivatives are used both for hedging and for taking views.
questions: A fund sells (writes) a call option on a stock it does not own. The theoretical maximum loss on this position is:
Limited to the premium received at the time of writing
Limited to the strike price of the option
Zero, because the option seller always keeps the premium
Unlimited, because the stock price can keep rising

A naked call writer must deliver the stock at the strike price however high the market price goes, so losses have no upper limit. The premium received is the writer's maximum gain, not the maximum loss.
A fund buys 1 lot of index futures (lot value ₹15 lakh) by paying an initial margin of ₹2 lakh. If the index rises 4%, the gain as a percentage of margin is closest to:
Gain = 4% × ₹15 lakh = ₹60,000. As a share of the ₹2 lakh margin, that is 30%. This shows how futures provide leveraged exposure: a small margin controls a much larger notional value.
A Category III fund wants to profit from a fall in the price of a stock it does not own. The standard way to do this in Indian markets is to:
Sell the stock's futures contract
Buy the stock in the cash market
Buy a call option on the stock
Subscribe to the stock's rights issue
Selling futures creates a short exposure that gains when the price falls. Buying the stock or a call option are bullish positions, and a rights issue adds to the holding.
In an interest rate swap, a fund that pays fixed and receives floating will benefit when:
Floating interest rates fall sharply after the swap starts
The fixed rate is reset to a higher level by the counterparty
Bond yields remain exactly unchanged for the full tenor
Floating interest rates rise above the fixed rate
Paying fixed and receiving floating gains when floating payments received exceed the fixed payments made. If floating rates fall, the fund receives less while still paying the same fixed rate.
A fund buys a stock at ₹800 and simultaneously buys a put option with strike ₹760 for a premium of ₹15. The maximum loss per share on the combined position is:
Below ₹760 the put offsets further falls, so the loss is the ₹40 drop to the strike plus the ₹15 premium = ₹55. This 'protective put' caps downside at a known cost.
Treasury bills are often held by Category III funds alongside derivative positions mainly because they:
Are near-cash, low-risk instruments useful as margin and liquidity buffers
Pay the highest coupon among all fixed income instruments issued in India today
Are equity-linked and increase the fund's market exposure
Cannot be pledged and therefore protect the fund from margin calls

T-bills are short-term sovereign instruments with minimal credit and interest rate risk, making them suitable collateral and cash management tools. They are issued at a discount and carry no coupon at all.
An option's 'time value' is best defined as:
The full premium paid for an at-the-money option
The part of the premium above the option's intrinsic value
The difference between strike price and futures price
The interest earned on the margin money deposited with the broker until expiry
Option premium = intrinsic value + time value. Time value reflects the chance that the option becomes more valuable before expiry, and it decays to zero by the expiry date.
A convertible bond is attractive to some hedge strategies because it:
Combines a fixed income claim with an embedded option to convert into equity
Carries no credit risk at all since it is always backed by a full government guarantee
Must be converted into shares on the date of issue
Is a pure equity instrument with voting rights from day one

A convertible pays interest like a bond but lets the holder convert into shares, so its value has a bond floor plus an equity option. Convertible arbitrage strategies try to exploit mispricing of that embedded option.

Modern Portfolio Theory and Capital Mark.overview: This chapter covers Markowitz's mean-variance framework and the Capital Asset Pricing Model. Key ideas include diversification and correlation, the efficient frontier, the minimum variance portfolio, the capital allocation line, the Capital Market Line, the Security Market Line, beta and systematic versus unsystematic risk. It also introduces criticisms and extensions such as multi-factor models and why hedge-fund returns often do not fit normal-distribution assumptions. Practise CAPM and portfolio beta calculations, and understand the difference between total risk (standard deviation) and market risk (beta).
questions: The risk-free rate is 6%, the expected market return is 13% and a stock's beta is 0.8. Under CAPM, its required return is:
CAPM: required return = Rf + beta × (Rm − Rf) = 6% + 0.8 × 7% = 6% + 5.6% = 11.6%. A beta below 1 implies a return below the market's 13%.
Adding a new asset to a portfolio will reduce portfolio risk the most when its correlation with the existing portfolio is:
Exactly +1
Slightly positive
Strongly negative
Equal to the asset's beta

The lower the correlation, the greater the diversification benefit. Perfect positive correlation gives no risk reduction, while negative correlation lets losses in one holding be offset by gains in the other.
Portfolios lying below the efficient frontier are:
Unattainable, because no combination of the available assets can ever produce them
Sub-optimal, because another portfolio offers higher return for the same risk
Optimal for investors who are highly risk-averse
Always made up only of the risk-free asset
The efficient frontier shows the best return for each level of risk. Anything below it is dominated. Portfolios above the frontier are the ones that cannot be achieved.
Under CAPM, which risk is rewarded with a higher expected return?
Company-specific risk that can be diversified away
Total risk measured by standard deviation alone
Systematic risk measured by beta
Liquidity risk of the investor's own bank account
CAPM assumes investors hold diversified portfolios, so only non-diversifiable market risk earns a premium. Unsystematic risk can be eliminated by diversification and so earns no extra return.
The Security Market Line shows a stock's required return of 12%, but analysts expect 15%. According to CAPM, the stock is:
Overvalued, with a negative alpha of 3%
Correctly priced because it lies on the CML
Risk-free because its return exceeds the requirement
Undervalued, with a positive alpha of 3%
When expected return exceeds the CAPM-required return, the stock plots above the SML and appears underpriced. The 3% excess is its alpha. That does not make the stock risk-free.
Many hedge-fund return series show negative skewness and fat tails. The main implication for risk measurement is that:
Standard deviation alone may understate the chance of large losses
The Sharpe ratio becomes a perfect and complete measure of the fund's risk-adjusted return
Beta to the equity market will always be exactly zero
Returns can be assumed to follow a normal distribution

Fat tails mean extreme outcomes happen more often than a normal distribution predicts, and negative skew means big losses are more likely than big gains. Measures relying on standard deviation can therefore mislead.
A fund has ₹100 crore, with 70% in a portfolio of beta 1.2 and the rest in cash (beta 0). It then sells index futures worth ₹40 crore. The fund's approximate beta becomes:
Equity beta exposure = 0.7 × 1.2 = 0.84. Short futures of ₹40 crore on ₹100 crore reduce beta by 0.40. Net beta = 0.84 − 0.40 = 0.44.
Arbitrage Pricing Theory and multi-factor models extend CAPM mainly by:
Allowing several systematic risk factors to explain expected returns
Assuming that the market portfolio is the one and only source of priced risk for all assets
Removing the need for any risk-free rate in pricing
Proving that diversification increases unsystematic risk
Multi-factor models use factors such as size, value, momentum or macro variables, each with its own sensitivity. CAPM uses only one factor, the market portfolio.

AIFs in India and Its Suitability.overview: This chapter explains how SEBI classifies Alternative Investment Funds into Categories I, II and III, what distinguishes Category III (diverse or complex trading strategies, use of leverage, investment in listed and unlisted derivatives), and how these funds compare with mutual funds and PMS. It also covers who should invest: high-net-worth and institutional investors able to bear risk, illiquidity and higher fees. Focus on suitability — matching strategy risk, lock-in and liquidity to investor profile — and on the minimum investment and investor-count rules in concept.
questions: A Category III AIF is distinguished from Category I and II AIFs mainly because it:
May use leverage and complex trading strategies, including in listed securities and derivatives
Is required to invest only in start-ups and social ventures
Can only invest in unlisted debt of infrastructure companies and in government-approved social sector projects
Is not allowed to raise money from domestic investors at all

Category III covers funds that employ diverse or complex trading strategies and may employ leverage, such as hedge funds and long-short funds. Category I covers start-up, social and infrastructure-focused funds, and Category II covers private equity and private debt.
Which investor is generally most suitable for a market-neutral Category III fund?
A retiree who needs a fixed monthly income and full safety of capital from the investment
A family office seeking returns with low correlation to equity markets
A first-time investor with ₹50,000 in savings
A college student who wants daily liquidity for expenses

Market-neutral funds aim to generate returns that are independent of market direction, which suits sophisticated investors wanting diversification. They need high minimum ticket sizes and are not suitable for investors who need capital safety or regular income.
Compared with an equity mutual fund, a long-only Category III AIF typically allows the manager to:
Offer the scheme to retail investors with a ₹500 SIP
Guarantee a minimum return to investors each year
Avoid all disclosure of fees to investors
Run a more concentrated portfolio with fewer diversification limits

Mutual funds face strict concentration limits for retail protection. Category III AIFs, aimed at sophisticated investors, can hold more concentrated positions, but still disclose fees and cannot guarantee returns.
An investor wants exposure to a strategy that profits mainly from mispricing between cash and futures markets. The most relevant AIF category is:
Category III, which covers trading and arbitrage strategies
Category I, which covers venture capital and SME funds
Category II, which covers private equity and private debt
A Social Impact Fund under Category I
Cash-futures arbitrage is a trading strategy in listed markets, which falls within Category III. Categories I and II mainly invest in unlisted companies with long holding periods.
A key suitability risk of recommending a leveraged Category III fund to a client is that:
Leverage always guarantees higher returns than the benchmark
Leverage removes the need for any risk management because borrowed money always boosts the final return
Losses can be magnified beyond what the client expects from the market move
Leveraged funds cannot ever fall below their initial NAV
Leverage magnifies both gains and losses. A client who does not understand this can face drawdowns larger than the underlying market fall, so suitability assessment must cover loss-bearing capacity.
Why are AIFs restricted to investors with large minimum commitments?
To limit participation to investors who can bear complex risks and illiquidity
To ensure that the returns delivered by AIFs are always higher than those of comparable mutual funds
Because AIFs are exempt from all SEBI regulation
To allow AIFs to be listed on the main board of exchanges
High minimum ticket sizes act as a filter for sophistication and capacity to absorb losses. AIFs remain SEBI-regulated, and a high ticket size does not imply superior returns.
Which pair correctly matches an AIF strategy with its usual category?
Venture capital fund — Category III
Private debt fund — Category I
Infrastructure fund — Category III
Long-short equity fund — Category III

Long-short equity is a classic hedge-fund style strategy and falls in Category III. Venture capital and infrastructure funds belong to Category I, while private debt and private equity sit in Category II.
A client with a ₹3 crore portfolio wants to put ₹2.5 crore into a single high-volatility Category III fund. The most appropriate response is to:
Accept the investment as proposed, since the client comfortably meets the minimum ticket size for AIFs
Advise borrowing more money to increase the allocation further
Recommend the fund because past returns have been strong
Explain concentration risk and suggest a smaller allocation suited to the overall plan

Meeting the minimum investment does not make a large concentrated allocation suitable. Putting over 80% of wealth in one volatile fund creates excessive risk, so the investor should be guided to a proportionate allocation.

AIF Ecosystem.overview: This chapter describes the participants around a Category III AIF: sponsor, investment manager, trustee or designated partners, custodian, prime broker, fund administrator and registrar, auditor, valuer, legal advisors, distributors and investors. Learners should know who does what — for example, who holds assets, who computes NAV, who provides financing and stock borrowing, and who safeguards investors' interests. Understand the conflicts and counterparty risks that arise among these parties and why independent service providers improve governance.
questions: In a Category III AIF set up as a trust, the sponsor is best described as the entity that:
Holds the fund's securities in safe custody on behalf of investors
Provides audit opinions on the fund's annual financial statements
Sets up the AIF and contributes the required continuing interest
Acts as the exchange where the fund's units are traded
The sponsor establishes the fund and must keep a continuing interest, aligning it with investors. Custody, audit and trading venues are provided by separate parties.
A prime broker typically provides a Category III fund with:
Statutory audit and tax filing for the fund's investors
Registration of the fund with SEBI and filing of all regulatory reports on the manager's behalf
Financing, securities lending and consolidated clearing services
Independent valuation of unlisted securities for NAV purposes
Prime brokers bundle services such as margin financing, stock borrowing for short sales, clearing and reporting. Audit, registration and independent valuation are performed by other parties.
Why does SEBI require a custodian to be appointed for AIFs?
To decide which stocks the fund should buy or sell
To keep the fund's securities separate from the manager for investor protection
To guarantee investors against any fall in NAV
To market the fund's units to new investors
Independent custody reduces the risk that assets are misused, as the manager cannot directly control safekeeping. The custodian does not make investment decisions or guarantee returns.
A distributor of a Category III AIF learns that the fund pays higher trail commission than another suitable fund. The distributor should:
Recommend the higher-paying fund without telling the client
Rebate part of the commission secretly to win the client
Recommend based on client suitability and disclose the commission received
Avoid discussing fees altogether because AIF investors are sophisticated and can find out for themselves
Distributors must put suitability first and disclose the commission they earn so the investor can judge any conflict. Hidden commissions or secret rebates breach conduct norms.
The role of the fund administrator in an open-ended Category III fund includes:
Selecting the fund's long and short positions every day
Providing leverage to the fund through margin loans
Approving the fund's registration as an AIF
Maintaining fund accounts and processing subscriptions and redemptions

Administrators handle accounting, investor records, capital activity and NAV-related work. Portfolio decisions belong to the manager, financing comes from the prime broker and registration is granted by SEBI.
Concentrating all prime brokerage with a single provider exposes a fund to:
Market risk from a sudden fall in the Nifty index
Counterparty risk if that provider faces financial distress
Inflation risk on the fund's cash holdings
Currency risk on a purely rupee portfolio
If the sole prime broker fails, the fund's collateral and positions may be frozen. Many funds use multiple prime brokers to diversify this counterparty exposure.
The investment manager of an AIF is primarily responsible for:
Making investment decisions in line with the fund documents and regulations
Safekeeping of all securities held by the fund in its demat account and settling every trade
Certifying the fund's accounts as the statutory auditor
Resolving investor complaints as the regulator
The manager runs the portfolio and must follow the private placement memorandum and SEBI rules. Custody, statutory audit and regulation are separate roles.
A Category III fund appoints an auditor who is a close relative of the fund manager. The main concern is that:
The fund's returns will automatically fall
The auditor's independence may be compromised
SEBI will cancel the fund's registration immediately
The custodian will be unable to hold the fund's securities
Auditors must be independent so they can challenge the manager's accounts and valuations. A close relationship creates a conflict that weakens the assurance investors receive.

AIF Structuring.overview: This chapter explains how Category III AIFs are legally and economically structured. It covers the legal forms (trust, LLP, company, body corporate), open-ended versus close-ended funds, schemes under one registration, master-feeder and parallel structures, classes of units, lock-ins and redemption terms, and how commitment and drawdown work for close-ended funds. Pay attention to how structure affects taxation, investor rights, liquidity and fairness between investors entering at different times.
questions: The most common legal form used for AIFs in India is a:
Public limited company listed on an exchange
Cooperative society registered with a state
Sole proprietorship of the fund manager
Trust registered under the Indian Trusts Act
Most Indian AIFs are set up as trusts because of flexibility and familiarity with pass-through and trustee-based governance. LLPs and companies are permitted but less common.
In a master-feeder structure, the feeder fund:
Pools money from investors and invests it into the master fund
Makes all trades directly while the master only holds cash
Acts as the custodian for the master fund's assets
Lends money to the master fund at a fixed rate
Feeders collect capital, often from different investor groups, and channel it into one master fund that runs the portfolio. This allows one strategy to serve several investor types efficiently.
A close-ended Category III fund calls only 30% of committed capital at the first close. The remaining commitments will be drawn:
Automatically from the investor's bank account each month
Only if the fund's NAV falls below the first-close NAV
Through later drawdown notices as investment opportunities arise
From the sponsor, since investors are required to pay only the first instalment of their commitment
Commitment-based funds draw capital in stages via drawdown notices. Investors are legally bound to meet calls up to their commitment; the sponsor does not cover investor shortfalls.
Issuing different classes of units within a Category III fund is commonly used to:
Avoid disclosing the portfolio to any investor
Give some investors a guaranteed share of profits
Bypass the minimum investment requirement
Offer different fee structures or terms to different investor groups
Unit classes allow differences in fees, currency or lock-in while sharing a portfolio. They must be disclosed and cannot be used to guarantee returns or evade regulatory minimums.
An open-ended Category III fund receives large subscriptions immediately after a sharp NAV rise. Fair treatment of existing investors in performance-fee calculation is mainly addressed through:
Converting the fund to a close-ended structure
Suspending NAV calculation for a quarter
Paying new investors a bonus in units
Equalisation or series accounting

Equalisation or series accounting ensures each investor pays performance fees only on gains they actually earned. Without it, incoming investors may pay fees on gains they did not enjoy, or escape fees on later gains.
A parallel fund structure is generally used when:
The manager wants to avoid all investor reporting
Different investor groups need separate vehicles that invest side by side
The fund wants to invest only in a single stock
Investors want to redeem their units every day without giving any notice to the manager
Parallel funds invest alongside the main fund in proportion, often to accommodate tax, regulatory or currency needs of particular investors. They do not reduce reporting obligations.
Why might a manager choose a close-ended rather than open-ended structure for a Category III fund holding less liquid listed small-caps?
To charge a higher management fee that open-ended Category III funds are not allowed to charge
To match fund liquidity with the time needed to exit the holdings
To avoid having any NAV computed during the tenure
To be able to accept retail investors with small tickets
Illiquid holdings can be hard to sell quickly to meet redemptions. A close-ended structure avoids forced selling and liquidity mismatch, while NAV reporting and investor minimums still apply.
A Category III AIF launches a new scheme under its existing registration. Which document must be filed with SEBI for the new scheme?
A red herring prospectus for listing the scheme's units on the main board of a stock exchange
A scheme information document approved by AMFI
A fresh certificate of incorporation from the ROC
A placement memorandum for the scheme, filed through a merchant banker
AIF schemes are launched through a private placement memorandum, filed with SEBI via a merchant banker. Prospectuses and scheme information documents relate to public issues and mutual funds.

Fee Structure and Fund Performance.overview: This chapter covers how Category III funds charge investors and how their performance is measured. Fee items include management fees, performance fees (carry), hurdle rates, catch-up, high-water marks, set-up and operating expenses and distribution commissions. Performance tools include absolute and annualised returns, time-weighted and money-weighted returns, drawdown, Sharpe, Sortino, Treynor, information ratio and alpha. Practise computing net-of-fee returns and risk-adjusted ratios, and understand which measure suits which situation.
questions: A fund's NAV peaked at ₹150, fell to ₹120, then recovered to ₹135. A high-water mark of ₹150 means the manager can charge a performance fee:
On the ₹15 recovery from ₹120 to ₹135
On any positive return in the calendar year
Only on gains after NAV rises above ₹150
On the full NAV every quarter
A high-water mark ensures performance fees are paid only on new highs, so investors do not pay twice for recovering earlier losses. The ₹120 to ₹135 recovery attracts no performance fee.
A fund returned 14% with a downside deviation of 8%. The risk-free rate is 6%. Its Sortino ratio is:
Sortino = (return − risk-free) / downside deviation = (14 − 6) / 8 = 1.00. It penalises only harmful volatility, unlike the Sharpe ratio, which uses total standard deviation.
A fund's NAV goes from ₹100 to ₹140 and then falls to ₹105. The maximum drawdown is:
Maximum drawdown is the largest peak-to-trough fall: (140 − 105) / 140 = 25%. It is measured from the peak, not the starting NAV, so it is not 35% or 5%.
A gross return of 20% is subject to a 2% management fee and then a 20% performance fee on the remaining return (no hurdle). The approximate net return is:
After the management fee, return = 20 − 2 = 18%. Performance fee = 20% × 18 = 3.6%. Net = 18 − 3.6 = 14.4%. This simplified sequence ignores timing and compounding of fee accruals.
A 'hurdle rate' in a performance fee arrangement means:
The manager's management fee is waived in a falling market
The manager earns a performance fee only if returns exceed a set minimum
The investor must pay a fixed fee every year regardless of how the fund has actually performed
Redemptions are allowed only above a certain NAV level
A hurdle sets a minimum return investors must receive before carry applies. It protects investors from paying performance fees on modest returns they could earn elsewhere.
When should money-weighted return (IRR) rather than time-weighted return be used to judge performance?
When the manager controls the timing of investor cash flows, as in drawdown funds
When investors themselves decide when to subscribe and redeem, as in a typical open-ended fund
When comparing two funds with exactly identical cash flows each day
When the fund has no cash flows during the whole year

IRR reflects the timing and size of cash flows. In close-ended drawdown funds, the manager decides when to call and return money, so IRR is appropriate. TWR suits open-ended funds where investors control flows.
Two funds have the same Sharpe ratio. Fund X has a lower beta than Fund Y. For an investor holding a well-diversified main portfolio, Fund X will have a:
Lower Treynor ratio, regardless of excess return
Higher standard deviation than Fund Y
Higher Treynor ratio, if both have the same excess return
Lower information ratio by definition
Treynor = excess return / beta. With the same excess return, the fund with lower beta earns more per unit of market risk. Sharpe uses total risk, so the two ratios can rank funds differently.
A fund returned 11% against a benchmark return of 9%, with tracking error of 5%. The information ratio is:
Information ratio = active return / tracking error = (11 − 9) / 5 = 0.40. It measures how consistently the manager adds value relative to the benchmark.

Indices and Benchmarking.overview: This chapter explains how market indices are built and how Category III funds should choose benchmarks. Topics include price-weighted, equal-weighted and free-float market-cap-weighted indices, price return versus total return indices, rebalancing and reconstitution, survivorship bias in hedge-fund indices, and the qualities of a good benchmark (specified in advance, investable, measurable, appropriate to the strategy). Focus on matching benchmarks to strategies such as long-short or arbitrage, and on SEBI's push for standardised benchmarking of AIF performance.
questions: A good benchmark for a Category III fund should be:
Chosen after the year-end, based on whichever index the fund managed to beat during that year
The same broad equity index for every type of AIF strategy
Changed every quarter to show the fund in the best light
Specified in advance, measurable and appropriate to the fund's strategy
A valid benchmark is unambiguous, investable, measurable and set before performance is evaluated. Choosing or changing it after the fact misleads investors about the manager's skill.
Survivorship bias in a hedge-fund database index tends to:
Overstate the average returns of the hedge-fund universe
Understate returns because only failed funds are included
Have no effect because all funds report every month
Reduce the measured volatility to zero
Funds that close, often after poor performance, drop out of databases, leaving mostly survivors. The index then looks better than the true experience of investors across all funds.
In a free-float market capitalisation weighted index, a company with large promoter holding will have a weight that is:
Higher than its weight by total market capitalisation
Equal for all companies in the index
Based only on its share price
Lower than its weight by total market capitalisation

Free-float weighting counts only shares available for trading, excluding promoter and locked-in holdings. Companies with high promoter stakes therefore get a smaller weight than total market cap suggests.
A cash-futures arbitrage Category III fund benchmarks itself against the Nifty 50 TRI. Why is this inappropriate?
The fund's returns resemble money-market returns, not equity market returns
The Nifty 50 TRI does not include dividends
Arbitrage funds are not allowed by SEBI to use or disclose any benchmark index at all
The Nifty 50 contains only 10 stocks

An arbitrage fund locks in the spread between cash and futures, giving low-risk, debt-like returns. Comparing it with an equity index is misleading; a liquid or arbitrage index is more suitable. The TRI does include dividends.
An equal-weighted index, compared with a market-cap weighted one, gives:
More influence to smaller companies in the index
Almost all influence to the largest companies
Influence based on each stock's share price
No role to index rebalancing
Equal weighting assigns the same weight to every constituent, so smaller companies matter more than under cap weighting. It also requires regular rebalancing to restore equal weights.
Index 'reconstitution' refers to:
Recalculating the index only for dividends
Converting a price return index into a currency-adjusted index for overseas investors
Suspending the index during market holidays
Changing the list of constituents according to the index rules
Reconstitution periodically adds and removes constituents based on criteria such as size and liquidity. Rebalancing adjusts weights of existing constituents. Both affect funds tracking the index.
A long-short equity fund that is typically 40% net long could reasonably construct a blended benchmark of:
40% equity index TRI and 60% money-market index
100% equity index TRI with double leverage
100% gold price index
60% equity index and 40% real estate index
A blended benchmark matching the fund's typical net exposure gives a fairer test of stock-selection skill. A full equity benchmark would penalise or flatter the fund depending on market direction.
An index provider caps the weight of any single stock in a sector index. The main purpose of such capping is to:
Limit concentration so the index stays diversified
Guarantee that the index will rise faster than the broad market every year
Give the largest company a bigger weight than its free-float market value
Remove the need for periodic index rebalancing or reconstitution

Without caps, one or two dominant companies can drive a sector index, making it concentrated and harder for funds to replicate within their own limits. Capping keeps the index diversified; it does not promise returns or remove rebalancing.

Legal Documentation and Negotiations.overview: This chapter covers the documents that govern a Category III AIF and the terms investors negotiate. Key documents include the private placement memorandum (PPM), the indenture of trust or LLP agreement, the contribution or subscription agreement, investment management agreement and side letters. Terms to understand include lock-ins, gates, side pockets, key-person clauses, most-favoured-nation clauses, fee terms, removal of the manager and reporting rights. Focus on what each clause protects and the conflicts it may create between investors.
questions: A 'key person' clause in an AIF's documents typically gives investors the right to:
Suspend new investments or exit if named key managers leave the fund
Appoint their own fund manager every year
Receive a fixed dividend every quarter
Avoid paying any management fee in a year in which the fund's NAV declines
Investors often back a fund because of specific individuals. A key person clause protects them by triggering suspension or other remedies if those people depart or stop devoting enough time.
A large investor negotiates a lower management fee through a side letter. A most-favoured-nation (MFN) clause would allow other investors to:
Cancel their commitments without notice
Take over management of the fund
Receive the large investor's share of profits
Elect to receive similar terms granted to comparable investors
An MFN clause lets eligible investors see and opt into better terms given to others of similar size or type. It addresses fairness concerns created by side letters.
The private placement memorandum of a Category III fund is primarily meant to:
Guarantee that the fund will meet its target return
Disclose the strategy, risks, fees, conflicts and terms to prospective investors
Replace the need for any trust deed, contribution agreement or investment management agreement
Serve as an advertisement to the general public
The PPM is the main disclosure document for an AIF. It must be balanced and comprehensive, cannot promise returns, and AIFs cannot be marketed to the general public.
A fund's documents permit the manager to 'gate' redemptions at 15% of NAV per quarter. During a crisis, investors ask for 40% of NAV. The likely outcome is:
All redemptions are paid in full immediately
The fund is wound up automatically
Redemptions are scaled back proportionately, with the rest carried forward
Only the earliest requests received are paid in full and all the later requests are cancelled
A gate limits total redemptions in a period to protect remaining investors from fire sales. Requests above the gate are usually met pro rata and carried forward to later periods.
Investors in a Category III fund worry that the manager may materially change the fund's strategy after they invest. SEBI's framework addresses this by requiring that:
The manager may change the strategy freely as long as returns stay positive
Only the custodian needs to be told about any change in investment strategy
Strategy changes are banned for the full tenure, even with unanimous approval
Material changes need investor consent, and dissenters get an exit option

Changes to material terms of the placement memorandum require approval from a specified majority of investors, and those who disagree must be offered an exit. This protects investors who chose the fund for its stated strategy.
Investor rights to remove the manager 'without cause' usually require:
A decision by the fund's custodian alone
Approval by a specified super-majority of investors
Consent of the stock exchange
No approval, since any single investor can do it
Removal without cause is a serious step, so documents typically require a high percentage of investor commitments to agree. This balances investor protection with stability of management.
Before signing a contribution agreement, an investor should carefully check the 'indemnification' clause because it determines:
The fund's annual target return
The list of stocks the fund will buy
When the fund bears costs of claims against the manager
The custodian's fee structure

Indemnification can require the fund, and therefore investors, to pay legal costs and losses arising from claims against the manager. Investors negotiate carve-outs for fraud, gross negligence or wilful misconduct.
Side letters with preferential terms for some investors raise the concern that:
Other investors may be disadvantaged without knowing the terms
The fund's NAV cannot be computed
The PPM becomes legally void
The fund can no longer use leverage
Preferential liquidity or information rights may harm other investors, for example by letting some exit earlier. SEBI expects disclosure of such arrangements and fair treatment of all investors.

Investment Strategies.overview: This chapter surveys the strategies used by Category III funds: long-only and long-short equity, market-neutral, pairs trading, statistical and quantitative strategies, merger and event-driven arbitrage, cash-futures arbitrage, volatility and options strategies, fixed income relative value, global macro and managed futures. Learners should understand each strategy's source of return, its main risks, typical leverage and exposure, and how gross and net exposure are computed. Expect scenario questions describing a position and asking which strategy it represents or how it performs in a given market move.
questions: Company A announces it will acquire Company B at ₹500 per share in cash; B trades at ₹470. A merger arbitrage fund buys B. Its main risk is that:
The broad equity market rises 5% next week
B's price moves up to exactly ₹500 on completion
Interest rates on government bonds fall slightly
The deal fails and B's price falls back sharply

Merger arbitrage earns the spread if the deal completes. The key risk is deal failure from regulatory, financing or shareholder issues, which can send the target's price down well below the current price.
A fund has NAV ₹200 crore, long positions of ₹240 crore and short positions of ₹160 crore. Its gross exposure as a percentage of NAV is:
Gross exposure = (long + short) / NAV = (240 + 160) / 200 = 200%. Net exposure would be (240 − 160) / 200 = 40%. Gross shows total risk and leverage, net shows directional bias.
A volatility-selling strategy that writes options regularly tends to show:
Occasional large gains with frequent small losses
No losses at all over time, because the option premiums received are always earned by the seller
Returns that rise sharply in market crashes
Steady small gains with occasional large losses in market shocks

Option sellers collect premium most of the time but face large pay-outs when markets move sharply. This creates negatively skewed returns, often described as 'picking up coins in front of a steamroller'.
A statistical arbitrage strategy typically relies on:
Long-term ownership of a single unlisted company
Physical storage of agricultural commodities
Quantitative models exploiting short-term price relationships across many securities
Lending money to infrastructure projects for ten years or more and holding the loans to maturity
Stat-arb uses models to identify small, temporary mispricings, often betting that prices will revert to historical relationships. Positions are many, short-dated and usually close to market-neutral.
Managed futures or CTA-style strategies typically make money by:
Collecting rental income from commercial property
Following price trends across futures markets, both long and short
Buying start-ups and holding them for a decade
Holding only fixed deposits until maturity

Trend-following strategies go long rising markets and short falling ones across equity, bond, currency and commodity futures. They have historically performed well in sustained trending periods, including some crises.
A fund buys a 10-year government bond and sells a 5-year government bond expecting the yield curve to flatten. This is an example of:
Fixed income relative value
Merger arbitrage
Long-only small-cap investing
Distressed equity investing

Relative value trades take offsetting positions in related instruments to profit from changes in their relationship, here the spread between 10-year and 5-year yields, rather than the direction of rates.
A long-short equity fund is 120% long and 90% short. If the whole market falls 10% and both books move with the market, the approximate impact on NAV is:
Net exposure = 120% − 90% = 30%. A 10% market fall costs about 30% × 10% = 3% of NAV. The long book loses 12% of NAV and the short book gains 9%, netting to −3%.
A global macro manager believes the RBI will cut rates more than the market expects. A consistent trade would be to:
Buy long-duration government bonds
Sell long-duration government bonds
Buy floating-rate notes only
Short bank fixed deposits
If rates fall more than expected, bond yields fall and long-duration bond prices rise most. Selling bonds or buying floating-rate notes would not benefit from an unexpected rate cut.

Governance of Funds and Due Diligence.overview: This chapter covers how Category III funds are governed and how investors assess them. Governance topics include the roles of the trustee, investment committee, compliance officer, conflicts of interest policies, trade allocation, personal trading rules and code of conduct. Due diligence includes investment due diligence (strategy, edge, risk management, track record) and operational due diligence (service providers, valuation, cash controls, IT and cyber security, compliance). Focus on red flags and on the practical questions an investor should ask.
questions: Operational due diligence on a Category III fund focuses mainly on:
Controls, service providers, valuation and cash-movement processes
The fund's expected return for the next year
The manager's views on the economy
Which stocks the manager plans to buy next

Operational due diligence checks whether the fund's infrastructure can protect assets and produce reliable numbers. Many hedge fund failures stem from operational weaknesses rather than poor investment ideas.
Which of the following is a red flag in due diligence of a Category III fund?
The fund uses an established custodian and independent administrator
The fund has a written personal trading policy for staff
The manager uses a small, unknown auditor and refuses to share audited accounts
The fund's risk management team reports to someone other than the portfolio manager who takes positions
An obscure auditor and refusal to share audited statements prevent verification of assets and returns. The other choices are signs of good governance and independence.
A fund manager's employees trade personally in stocks the fund also trades. The best governance control is:
Allowing staff to trade freely if they disclose annually
Banning only the fund manager from personal trading
Requiring staff to trade only after the fund's NAV rises
Pre-clearance of personal trades and restricted lists
Pre-clearance and restricted lists prevent front-running and misuse of fund information. Annual disclosure alone comes too late to stop conflicts arising.
A manager runs two funds with different fee rates and allocates the best IPO allotments to the higher-fee fund. This is a breach of:
The custodian's safekeeping duties
Fair trade allocation among clients
The auditor's independence requirement
The fund's leverage limit
Managers must allocate trades fairly according to a pre-defined policy. Favouring the fund that pays more fees harms the other fund's investors and is a conflict of interest.
Why do investors prefer a fund's risk management function to be independent of portfolio managers?
So that portfolio managers can override the risk limits whenever markets become volatile
So that the fund can avoid regulatory reporting
So that risk limits can be enforced without pressure from those taking the risk
So that the risk team can pick the stocks
An independent risk function can challenge positions and escalate breaches. If it reports to the portfolio manager, limits may be ignored when they are most needed.
During investment due diligence, an investor finds that the fund's track record comes from a previous employer. The investor should check:
Only that the returns were above the Nifty 50
Whether the manager has a large social media following and is often quoted in the financial press
That the PPM contains the word 'guaranteed'
Whether the record is attributable to this manager and verified independently
Portable track records may include work by other team members or different conditions. Investors should verify attribution and accuracy rather than accept headline numbers.
A Category III fund's compliance officer is expected to:
Decide the fund's asset allocation
Approve the custodian's own audit
Market the fund to new investors
Monitor adherence to SEBI regulations and report non-compliance
The compliance officer ensures that the fund follows regulations and its own documents, and reports breaches. Investment decisions and marketing are outside this role.
Why is cyber-security and data protection now part of operational due diligence?
Because SEBI requires all AIFs to trade only online
Breaches can lead to theft of assets, data or trading strategies
Because cyber-security improves investment returns directly
Because it replaces the need for a custodian
Funds hold sensitive investor data and proprietary models, and payment fraud is a real risk. Weak cyber controls can cause losses that have nothing to do with market risk.

Valuation.overview: This chapter explains how a Category III fund values its holdings to compute NAV. It covers the principles of fair value, mark-to-market for liquid listed securities and exchange-traded derivatives, valuation of thinly traded or suspended securities, unlisted and OTC instruments, the role of independent valuers and valuation committees, and SEBI's expectations on valuation policy and independence. Focus on why consistent, independent valuation matters for fair treatment of incoming and outgoing investors and for performance-fee calculations.
questions: If a Category III fund overstates its NAV, which group is harmed directly?
Only the fund's custodian
Nobody, because NAV errors cancel out
Remaining and incoming investors, while redeeming investors are overpaid
Only the stock exchange
An inflated NAV pays redeeming investors more than their fair share and charges new investors too much, leaving the fund poorer. It can also lead to excess performance fees.
A listed stock held by the fund is suspended from trading for two months. The most appropriate valuation approach is to:
Keep using the last traded price indefinitely without any review until trading in the stock resumes
Value it at zero immediately in every case
Value it at the fund's purchase price
Fair value it using a documented method, such as recent fundamentals or comparables
A suspended stock's last price may be stale. The valuation policy should require fair valuation using reasonable inputs, with documentation and oversight, rather than mechanical rules.
A fund holds an OTC interest rate swap with a bank. To value it independently, the administrator would most likely use:
The swap's original notional amount
The bank's own quote without any check
The fund manager's target value
A model based on current market yield curves
OTC swaps have no exchange price, so they are valued by discounting expected cash flows using current market curves. Relying only on the counterparty's or manager's numbers creates conflicts.
The 'fair value hierarchy' gives greatest reliability to valuations based on:
Management's internal estimates with no observable inputs
Prices of different assets in inactive markets
Quoted prices in active markets for identical assets
The original cost of the investment
Level 1 inputs — quoted prices for identical assets in active markets — are the most reliable. Level 3 inputs rely on unobservable assumptions and need greater scrutiny.
Why does a fund's valuation committee often include members outside the investment team?
To reduce the conflict arising because fees depend on NAV
To make NAV calculation faster each day
To avoid sharing valuations with auditors
Because portfolio managers are not allowed to see prices
Managers earn management and performance fees based on NAV, so they have an incentive to value high. Independent members help ensure valuations are objective and defensible.
A fund holds a large block of a small-cap stock equal to ten days' average trading volume. A conservative valuation practice might be to:
Value it at a premium to the market price because the fund's stake in the company is large
Exclude it from NAV until it is sold
Use the highest price of the past year
Consider a liquidity adjustment if the block cannot be sold at the quoted price
The quoted price may not be achievable for a large position. Valuation policies may permit a liquidity discount, applied consistently and disclosed, to reflect realistic exit value.
SEBI expects an AIF's valuation of investments to be carried out by:
Any investor who holds the most units
The distributor who sold the fund
The fund's tax consultant only
An independent valuer as per the valuation policy in the fund documents
SEBI requires valuations by independent valuers following the methodology disclosed in the placement memorandum. Distributors and investors have conflicts and lack the mandate.
A fund changes its valuation method for unlisted bonds in mid-year, which raises NAV by 3%. Investors should expect:
No disclosure at all, since a fund's valuation methods are confidential business information
Disclosure of the change, its reasons and its impact on NAV
An automatic waiver of performance fees for ten years
Immediate de-registration of the fund
Valuation methods should be applied consistently, and any change must be justified and disclosed to investors. Unexplained changes that lift NAV may hide performance problems.

Fund Monitoring, Reporting and Exit.overview: This chapter covers how a Category III fund monitors risk and reports to investors and SEBI, and how investors exit. Monitoring tools include exposure limits, leverage tracking, Value at Risk, stress testing, liquidity analysis and drawdown limits. Reporting covers NAV statements, portfolio and risk disclosures, periodic reports to investors and regulatory filings. Exit topics include redemptions in open-ended funds, winding up of close-ended funds, in-specie distributions and dealing with illiquid residual assets. Focus on interpreting risk measures and on fair treatment at exit.
questions: A fund's one-day 99% VaR is ₹5 crore. This means:
On 1 day in 100, losses are expected to exceed ₹5 crore
The fund can never lose more than ₹5 crore in a day
The fund will lose ₹5 crore on 99 days out of 100
The fund's average daily loss is ₹5 crore
VaR gives a loss threshold at a confidence level. At 99%, losses should exceed ₹5 crore on about 1% of days. VaR does not show how large those tail losses could be.
A fund's one-day VaR is ₹2 crore. Using the square-root-of-time rule, its approximate 25-day VaR is:
₹10 crore
₹50 crore
₹25 crore
₹4 crore
Under the square-root-of-time rule, VaR scales with the square root of the horizon: ₹2 crore × √25 = ₹2 crore × 5 = ₹10 crore. This assumes independent, identically distributed returns.
Which is a key limitation of Value at Risk?
It says nothing about the size of losses beyond the threshold
It cannot be calculated for equity portfolios
It always overstates risk in calm markets
It requires the fund to hold no derivatives, short positions or leverage at the time of calculation
VaR tells you the threshold but not how bad the tail can get. Expected shortfall (conditional VaR) and stress tests complement it by looking at losses beyond VaR.
Liquidity monitoring of an open-ended Category III fund mainly compares:
The fund's returns against the Nifty 50
How quickly holdings can be sold against likely redemption demands
The manager's salary against the fee income
The number of investors against the custodian's capacity
Funds must be able to meet redemptions without fire sales. Liquidity analysis maps the time needed to liquidate positions against expected and stressed outflows.
A close-ended Category III fund reaches the end of its tenure with some unlisted holdings unsold. One possible exit route permitted under SEBI's framework is:
Selling the assets to the sponsor at any price it chooses
In-specie distribution of the unsold assets to investors, with their consent
Extending the fund's tenure indefinitely without seeking any approval from the investors
Writing the assets off and charging investors a penalty

SEBI's framework for unliquidated investments allows options such as in-specie distribution or transfer to a liquidation scheme, subject to investor consent. Unilateral extension or related-party sales at arbitrary prices are not acceptable.
A stress test that applies the market moves of a past crisis to today's portfolio is called:
Monte Carlo simulation
Historical scenario analysis
Back-testing of a trading signal
Attribution analysis
Historical scenarios replay real past events, such as a market crash, to see how the current portfolio would fare. Monte Carlo uses random simulations, and attribution explains past returns.
Investors receive a report showing that a fund's leverage rose from 1.2x to 1.9x NAV in one quarter. A sensible investor action is to:
Ignore it because leverage always improves returns
Redeem immediately without asking any questions, since higher leverage always means fraud
Ask the manager why leverage rose and whether it fits the stated strategy
Ask the custodian to reduce leverage directly
A sharp rise in leverage may signal style drift or increased risk. Investors should seek explanation and check consistency with the PPM before deciding on action.
Expected shortfall (conditional VaR) is best described as:
The average loss in the worst cases beyond the VaR threshold
The smallest loss the fund can make in a year
The loss on the single best day of the year
The fund's expected return minus its fees
Expected shortfall averages the losses in the tail beyond VaR, giving a better view of extreme risk. It is increasingly preferred because it captures tail severity that VaR ignores.

Taxation.overview: This chapter explains how Category III AIFs and their investors are taxed in India. Unlike Category I and II, Category III AIFs do not enjoy statutory pass-through, so income is generally taxed at the fund level — for trusts, often through the representative assessee rules — and the characterisation of income (capital gains versus business income) significantly affects the rate. Learners should also understand GST on management fees, securities transaction tax, the treatment of derivative income, and tax issues for non-resident investors. Tax rates change with budgets, so focus on principles and check current rates.
questions: A key tax difference between Category III AIFs and Category I/II AIFs is that:
Category III funds are fully exempt from income tax
Category III income is always taxed only in investors' hands
Category III funds do not have statutory pass-through status
Category I and II funds pay tax at the maximum marginal rate
The Income-tax Act grants pass-through to Category I and II AIFs for non-business income. Category III funds lack this, so tax is generally paid at fund level, often through trustee-level taxation.
Income from frequent trading in futures and options by a Category III fund is most likely to be treated as:
Long-term capital gains
Business income
Income from house property
Exempt agricultural income
Derivative trading carried out as an activity is generally treated as non-speculative business income. That characterisation affects the applicable rate and how losses are set off.
GST is generally levied on:
Management and performance fees charged by the AIF manager
The investor's capital contribution to the fund
The sale proceeds of listed shares
Dividends received by the fund
Fund management is a service, so GST applies to fees charged by the manager. Capital contributions, share sale proceeds and dividends are not taxable supplies for GST.
Securities Transaction Tax (STT) is relevant to a Category III fund because it is:
A tax on the fund manager's personal salary
Levied on purchases and sales of listed securities and derivatives on exchanges
Payable only on unlisted debentures
A tax collected on investors' redemptions from bank fixed deposits and savings accounts
STT is charged on exchange-traded transactions in equity shares, equity-oriented units and derivatives. It adds to trading costs, which matters for high-turnover strategies.
For a Category III AIF set up as a determinate trust, where shares of beneficiaries are known, the tax is generally:
Waived entirely because trusts are charitable
Paid by the fund's custodian from its own funds, since the custodian holds the trust's assets
Assessed on the trustee as representative assessee in respect of each beneficiary's share
Postponed until the fund is wound up

For determinate trusts, the trustee is taxed as representative assessee in the same way and to the same extent as the beneficiaries would be. Indeterminate trusts can face tax at the maximum marginal rate.
Why does the characterisation of a Category III fund's equity gains as capital gains or business income matter?
Business income is completely exempt from tax in India
Capital gains are taxed only if the fund is listed abroad, while business income is never taxed in India
Capital gains on listed equity can attract concessional rates, while business income is taxed at normal rates
There is no difference since both are taxed identically
Capital gains on listed equity enjoy specific rates, often lower than the slab or maximum rates on business income. Funds therefore document their intention and holding pattern carefully.
A non-resident investor in a Category III AIF should check a tax treaty mainly because it may:
Allow the investor to skip KYC requirements
Affect how the investor's income from India is taxed or credited at home
Guarantee that the fund will never make a loss on the investor's capital in any year
Let the investor avoid SEBI's minimum investment
Double taxation avoidance agreements allocate taxing rights and provide relief for tax paid in India. They do not affect KYC, minimum investment or investment risk.
Because Category III tax rules and rates change with Union Budgets, the most reliable practice for an investor is to:
Assume last year's rates will apply forever
Check the current law and the fund's tax disclosures before investing
Rely on informal opinions shared on social media
Ignore taxes completely, since they never make any real difference to net returns over time
Tax can materially change post-tax returns. Investors should refer to current provisions and the PPM's tax section, and take professional advice where needed.

Regulatory Framework.overview: This chapter covers SEBI (Alternative Investment Funds) Regulations, 2012 and related circulars as they apply to Category III funds. Topics include registration, eligibility of sponsor and manager, minimum corpus and investment, maximum number of investors, continuing interest, investment conditions and concentration limits, leverage limits, valuation and NAV disclosure, the compliance and certification requirements for key investment team members, investor charter and grievance redressal, and SEBI's powers to inspect and penalise. Thresholds are revised from time to time, so revise the current circulars carefully.
questions: An AIF may raise money only through:
Public issue of units through a prospectus
Private placement to eligible investors
Daily retail SIPs through bank branches
Unsolicited cold-calls to the general public
AIFs are privately pooled vehicles and must raise money through private placement using a placement memorandum. Public advertising and retail offerings are not permitted.
Under the AIF Regulations, the minimum investment for an investor (other than accredited investors and certain employees/directors) is:
₹10 lakh
₹50 lakh
₹25 crore
₹1 crore
The general minimum is ₹1 crore per investor, with a lower ₹25 lakh limit for employees or directors of the AIF or its manager. Accredited investors can be exempted. ₹50 lakh is the PMS minimum.
An AIF scheme (other than an angel fund) cannot have more than how many investors?
SEBI caps each AIF scheme at 1,000 investors, keeping AIFs as private pools. Angel funds have a lower limit of 200 investors.
SEBI requires certain key investment team members of an AIF manager to obtain which certification?
The relevant NISM certification for AIF managers
A certificate from the Bar Council of India
An insurance agent licence from IRDAI
A chartered accountancy membership only

SEBI has made an NISM certification on AIF management mandatory for key investment team members of AIF managers, so they understand the regulations, strategies and risks. Other professional licences do not satisfy this requirement.
Leverage employed by a Category III AIF is subject to:
No limit at all since investors are sophisticated
Limits set by SEBI and disclosure to investors
Approval by the stock exchange for each trade
A ban, since Category III cannot borrow or use derivatives
Category III AIFs may use leverage, but SEBI caps gross exposure relative to NAV and requires disclosures of leverage to investors and the regulator.
Investors in an AIF who have a grievance not resolved by the manager may approach:
Only the civil court located in the city where the fund's trust is registered
SEBI's SCORES platform and, thereafter, online dispute resolution
The Reserve Bank of India's ombudsman
The fund's distributor as final authority
SEBI-registered AIFs are covered by SCORES, and investors can escalate further through the online dispute resolution mechanism. RBI's ombudsman covers banking services, not AIFs.
A Category III fund wants to invest a large share of its investable funds in a single listed company. It should first check:
Whether the investee company has more than 1,000 employees and a long operating history
Whether the company pays dividends every month
The custodian's personal opinion on the stock
SEBI's concentration limit on investment in one investee company
SEBI imposes a concentration cap per investee company for Category III funds, expressed relative to NAV or investable funds. The fund must comply regardless of the manager's conviction.
Which body grants registration to an AIF in India?
Association of Mutual Funds in India (AMFI)
Ministry of Corporate Affairs
Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI)
Reserve Bank of India
AIFs are registered and regulated by SEBI under the AIF Regulations, 2012. AMFI is the mutual fund industry body, and RBI regulates banks and NBFCs.

Investments.overview: This opening chapter explains what investing means, how it differs from saving and speculation, and the broad asset classes available to Indian investors: equity, debt, real estate, gold, cash and alternatives. It covers the risk–return trade-off, the time value of money, compounding, inflation and real returns, and the idea of matching investments to goals. For a PMS distributor, the key takeaway is that every product recommendation must start from the client's objectives, horizon and risk profile. Practise simple compounding and return calculations and be clear on the features of each asset class.
questions: ₹5 lakh invested at 9% per annum compounded annually will grow in 3 years to approximately:
₹6.48 lakh
₹6.35 lakh
₹6.62 lakh
₹5.45 lakh
Future value = 5 × (1.09)³ = 5 × 1.295 = ₹6.48 lakh. Simple interest would give only ₹6.35 lakh, because compounding earns interest on interest each year.
Which statement about the risk–return trade-off is generally correct?
Higher-risk assets always deliver higher returns every year
Low-risk assets typically offer the highest long-term returns
Assets with higher expected return usually carry higher risk
Risk and return have no relationship in financial markets

Investors demand compensation for bearing uncertainty, so riskier assets are priced to offer higher expected returns. Expected does not mean guaranteed: risky assets can underperform for long periods.
A client keeps ₹40 lakh in a savings account earning 3% while inflation is 6%. The main risk the client faces is:
Default risk of the bank in the short term
Erosion of purchasing power over time
High volatility in the account balance every day
Reinvestment risk from receiving coupons on bonds

With returns below inflation, the real value of savings falls each year. Bank deposits have low volatility, and deposit insurance limits default risk for smaller balances, but inflation erodes wealth.
Gold is often included in Indian portfolios mainly because it:
Pays a regular dividend like equity shares do
Has historically provided diversification and a hedge in times of stress
Is guaranteed by the government to rise in price every year, making it risk-free
Has no price volatility at all
Gold tends to have low or negative correlation with equities during crises and is seen as a store of value. It pays no income and its price can be volatile.
Using the Rule of 72, money growing at 8% per year doubles in about:
9 years
8 years
12 years
6 years
Rule of 72: years to double ≈ 72 ÷ rate = 72 ÷ 8 = 9 years. It is a quick approximation that works well for rates between about 6% and 12%.
A 'speculator' differs from an 'investor' mainly because the speculator:
Holds assets only for the long-term income they generate and their underlying fundamentals
Avoids any form of market risk by holding cash
Seeks large short-term gains from price movements, accepting high risk
Buys only government securities to maturity
Speculation is short-term and based on price movement with high risk. Investing focuses on fundamentals and long-term value creation, often with income.
An investor's 'time horizon' is important in asset allocation because:
Short horizons always favour small-cap equity funds
Longer horizons can absorb short-term volatility in growth assets
Time horizon alone decides the tax rate applicable on every investment the client makes
Horizon does not affect the choice of assets
With more time, temporary falls in equity have a chance to recover, so long-horizon investors can hold more growth assets. Short horizons call for stable, liquid assets.
Real estate as an investment is characterised by:
Daily liquidity at a transparent exchange price
Very small ticket sizes suitable for all investors
No transaction costs on purchase or sale
Low liquidity and large ticket sizes
Physical property is lumpy, slow to sell and involves stamp duty and other costs. REITs offer a more liquid, smaller-ticket route to the same asset class.

Introduction to Securities Markets.overview: This chapter describes the structure of Indian securities markets: primary and secondary markets, equity and debt segments, stock exchanges, clearing corporations, depositories and depository participants, brokers, custodians and the role of SEBI as regulator. It explains how trades are executed and settled, the T+1 settlement cycle, dematerialisation and the investor protection mechanisms available. For PMS distributors, understanding market infrastructure helps explain to clients how their securities are held and how trades flow from order to settlement.
questions: Which institution guarantees settlement of trades executed on a stock exchange in India?
The stock broker of the buyer
The depository participant of the seller
The company whose shares are traded
The clearing corporation acting as central counterparty
The clearing corporation becomes the buyer to every seller and the seller to every buyer (novation), guaranteeing settlement. Brokers and DPs are intermediaries but do not guarantee trades.
An investor who wants to hold shares in electronic form must open a demat account with a:
Registrar of companies
Stock exchange directly
Credit rating agency
Depository participant
Depository participants such as banks and brokers act as agents of NSDL or CDSL and open demat accounts for investors. Exchanges and rating agencies do not hold investor securities.
A company sells existing promoter shares to the public in an IPO through an offer for sale. The proceeds go to:
The company, to fund new projects
SEBI, as a listing fee
The selling promoters, not the company
The stock exchange, as transaction charges
In an offer for sale, existing shareholders sell their shares, so they receive the money. Only a fresh issue brings new capital into the company.
The main purpose of SEBI's investor protection fund maintained by exchanges is to:
Guarantee investors against any market losses suffered on shares bought through brokers
Pay dividends when companies make losses
Fund new IPOs of small companies
Compensate investors for claims arising from defaulting brokers
Investor protection funds compensate eligible investors when a member broker defaults, within set limits. They do not cover losses from price falls.
In the debt market, treasury bills are issued by the:
Reserve Bank of India on behalf of the Government of India
State Bank of India for its own funding
SEBI for market stability
Stock exchanges for liquidity
T-bills are short-term Central Government securities auctioned by the RBI as the government's debt manager. They are issued at a discount and redeemed at face value.
A 'limit order' to buy a share at ₹250 will be executed:
At whatever price the market is at
Only at ₹250 or a lower price
Only at a price above ₹250
Only at the day's closing price
A limit buy order sets the maximum price the buyer will pay. A market order executes at the best available price, which may be higher.
Which market segment helps companies raise fresh capital directly from investors?
Primary market
Secondary market
Derivatives market
Currency market
In the primary market securities are issued for the first time and money flows to the issuer. The secondary market provides liquidity for existing securities among investors.
Under T+1 settlement, a share sold on Monday (a trading day, with Tuesday also a trading day) will be settled on:
Tuesday
Monday itself
Wednesday
Friday
T+1 means settlement one trading day after the trade date. A Monday trade therefore settles on Tuesday, assuming it is a working day.

Investing in Stocks.overview: This chapter covers equity as an asset class: rights of shareholders, sources of equity returns (dividends and capital gains), and approaches to stock analysis. It explains fundamental analysis using economy, industry and company factors, valuation ratios (P/E, P/B, EV/EBITDA, dividend yield), financial statement metrics (ROE, debt-equity, margins), technical analysis basics, and investment styles such as growth, value, large-cap and small-cap. Practise ratio calculations and learn which ratio is most useful for which type of company.
questions: A company has net profit of ₹60 crore and shareholders' equity of ₹400 crore. Its return on equity is:
ROE = net profit ÷ shareholders' equity = 60 ÷ 400 = 15%. It shows how much profit the company generates for each rupee of shareholders' capital.
Price-to-book (P/B) ratio is generally most useful for valuing:
Banks and financial companies with large balance sheets
Early-stage software start-ups with few assets
Companies with negative book value
Firms whose value lies mainly in brands
For banks, assets and liabilities are mostly financial and marked close to market value, so book value is meaningful. Asset-light or brand-driven firms are poorly captured by book value.
An investor who buys stocks trading below their intrinsic value based on low P/E and P/B ratios follows which style?
Momentum investing
Growth investing
Value investing
Index investing
Value investors look for stocks priced cheaply relative to fundamentals, expecting the market to correct. Growth investors pay up for high expected earnings growth.
A company has total debt of ₹300 crore and equity of ₹200 crore. Its debt-equity ratio is:
Debt-equity = debt ÷ equity = 300 ÷ 200 = 1.5. A higher ratio indicates greater financial leverage and more fixed obligations, which raises risk in a downturn.
Equity shareholders have a claim on a company's assets on liquidation that is:
Ahead of all bank lenders
Equal to that of secured debenture holders
Guaranteed at the face value of their shares, ahead of unsecured creditors and suppliers
Residual, after all creditors and preference shareholders are paid
Equity holders are owners and rank last on liquidation. They benefit from unlimited upside but bear the first loss when the company fails.
Which economic factor is most likely to hurt the share prices of rate-sensitive sectors like real estate and automobiles?
A fall in crude oil prices
Strong growth in rural incomes
A cut in the repo rate
A sharp rise in interest rates
Higher rates raise borrowing costs for buyers of homes and vehicles, reducing demand and profits. Rate cuts and rising incomes usually help these sectors.
A stock trades at ₹900 with EPS of ₹45; its peer group trades at a P/E of 25. On P/E alone, the stock looks:
Expensive, at a P/E of 30
Cheaper than peers, at a P/E of 20
Fairly valued, at a P/E of 25
Cheaper, at a P/E of 15
P/E = 900 ÷ 45 = 20, below the peer P/E of 25. A lower P/E may indicate undervaluation, but it can also reflect weaker growth or higher risk, so further analysis is needed.
A bonus issue of 1:1 by a company generally results in:
An immediate doubling of the investor's wealth
A cash payment to every shareholder equal to the face value of the shares already held
Reduction in the number of shares held
Double the number of shares, with the share price adjusting roughly by half
A bonus issue capitalises reserves into new shares; it does not add value. The price adjusts so the total value of holdings stays roughly the same.

Investing in Fixed Income Securities.overview: This chapter explains bonds and other debt instruments: face value, coupon, maturity, yield to maturity, current yield, price–yield relationship, duration and convexity, credit ratings and spreads, and the main types of issuers in India (Government securities, state development loans, PSU and corporate bonds, commercial paper, certificates of deposit). Risks covered include interest rate risk, credit risk, reinvestment risk and liquidity risk. Practise simple yield and duration calculations and be able to explain to clients why bond prices fall when rates rise.
questions: A bond's price falls when market yields rise because:
The issuer stops paying coupons when rates rise
Its fixed coupons become less attractive than new bonds paying higher rates
The bond's face value is reduced by the regulator
Coupon payments become taxable at a higher rate whenever market interest rates rise
With yields higher, investors will buy an existing bond only at a lower price so that its yield matches the market. The issuer's obligations remain unchanged.
Which bond carries the highest reinvestment risk, other things being equal?
A zero-coupon bond held to maturity
A high-coupon bond paying interest frequently
A treasury bill held to maturity
A low-coupon bond with annual payment
Reinvestment risk arises when coupons must be reinvested at possibly lower rates. Bonds paying large, frequent coupons are most exposed; zero-coupon bonds have none if held to maturity.
