A 1-year bond with face value ₹1,000 and an annual coupon of 7% trades at ₹990. Its yield to maturity is closest to:
At maturity the investor receives ₹1,070 for ₹990 paid. YTM = 1,070 ÷ 990 − 1 = 8.08%. Current yield would be 70 ÷ 990 = 7.07%, which ignores the price gain.
A credit rating downgrade of a corporate bond from AA to A will most likely cause:
Its coupon to rise automatically
Its price to rise because risk is higher
Its price to fall as the credit spread widens
No change because ratings do not matter
A downgrade signals higher default risk, so investors demand a higher yield. With a fixed coupon, the bond's price must fall to deliver that higher yield.
Commercial paper in India is best described as:
Short-term unsecured promissory notes issued by companies
Long-term secured bonds issued by the Government of India through RBI auctions
Certificates issued by banks against deposits
Shares issued to employees at a discount
CP is a money-market instrument issued at a discount by highly rated corporates for short-term funding. Banks issue certificates of deposit, and the government issues T-bills and G-secs.
A bond fund has a modified duration of 3. If yields fall by 1%, the fund's value will change by approximately:
Price change ≈ −modified duration × yield change = −3 × (−1%) = +3%. When yields fall, prices rise in proportion to duration.
Government securities are considered free of credit risk but still carry:
Interest rate risk
Default risk
Equity market risk
Currency risk on rupee bonds
The Government of India is not expected to default on rupee debt, but G-sec prices change with interest rates, and long-dated G-secs can be quite volatile.
For two bonds with the same coupon and yield, the one with the longer maturity will have:
Lower duration and less price sensitivity
Exactly the same price sensitivity
No sensitivity to interest rates
Higher duration and greater price sensitivity
Longer maturity means cash flows are received further in the future, raising duration. That makes the bond's price more sensitive to changes in yield.

Derivatives.overview: This chapter introduces derivatives traded in India — forwards, futures, options and swaps — and their use by portfolio managers for hedging and portfolio rebalancing. Topics include underlying assets, lot size, margins and mark-to-market, cost of carry pricing, option terminology (call, put, strike, premium, intrinsic and time value, in/at/out of the money), basic option strategies and the risks of leverage. PMS can use derivatives only within regulatory limits, so focus on hedging uses and on explaining risks clearly to clients.
questions: A put option with strike ₹600 when the stock trades at ₹640 is:
Out of the money
In the money
At the money
Deep in the money
A put is in the money when the market price is below the strike. Here the price is above the strike, so exercising would not be profitable and the put is out of the money.
A futures position is marked to market daily, which means:
Gains and losses are settled each day through the margin account
The position can be closed only at expiry
The contract price stays fixed until expiry and there are no interim cash flows at all
Only the buyer pays margins, not the seller
Daily mark-to-market credits gains and debits losses to both parties' accounts, reducing default risk. Positions can be closed any time before expiry.
A trader buys a call with strike ₹1,200 for ₹35. At expiry the stock is at ₹1,220. The net result per share is:
Profit of ₹20
Loss of ₹15
Loss of ₹35
Profit of ₹55
Intrinsic value at expiry = 1,220 − 1,200 = ₹20. Net = 20 − 35 = −₹15. The option is in the money but not by enough to recover the premium.
A PMS client holds a diversified equity portfolio worth ₹1 crore with beta 1.0. To temporarily hedge against a market fall, the manager could:
Buy index futures worth ₹1 crore
Buy call options on the index
Sell index futures with notional value close to ₹1 crore
Sell the client's bank fixed deposits
Short index futures gain when the market falls, offsetting losses on the portfolio. Buying futures or calls increases market exposure rather than hedging it.
Spot price is ₹2,000, the annual cost of carry is 9% and the contract expires in 2 months. The theoretical futures price is approximately:
Futures ≈ spot × (1 + r × t) = 2,000 × (1 + 0.09 × 2/12) = 2,000 × 1.015 = ₹2,030. Futures usually trade above spot by the cost of carry.
Compared with an option buyer, an option seller (writer):
Pays the premium and has limited loss
Has no obligation if the buyer exercises
Receives the premium but faces potentially large losses
Faces no margin requirements
The writer collects the premium upfront and must perform if the buyer exercises. Losses can be large, so exchanges require writers to post margin.
The main difference between a forward and a futures contract is that futures are:
Customised and traded privately between two parties
Free of any margin requirement
Settled only by physical delivery of the underlying asset in all cases at expiry
Standardised and traded on an exchange with a clearing guarantee
Futures have standard lot sizes and expiry dates and are cleared through a clearing corporation. Forwards are bilateral, customised and carry counterparty risk.
Which statement about using derivatives in a PMS portfolio is most accurate?
They can be used to take unlimited leveraged bets on client money if the client agrees
They may be used within SEBI limits, for example for hedging and rebalancing
They are completely prohibited for all portfolio managers
They remove all risk from the portfolio
SEBI permits portfolio managers to use derivatives subject to limits and the client agreement, but not to leverage client portfolios. Hedging reduces, but never eliminates, risk.

Collective Investment Vehicles.overview: This chapter compares the main pooled and managed investment products in India: mutual funds (open and close-ended, active and passive, ETFs), Alternative Investment Funds (Categories I, II and III), Portfolio Management Services, REITs and InvITs, and the newer Specialised Investment Funds. Learners should know the structure, regulator, minimum investment, liquidity, transparency, costs and tax treatment of each, and how to position PMS against these alternatives for clients of different sizes and needs.
questions: A key structural feature of a mutual fund that is NOT present in a PMS account is that:
Investors' holdings are fully customised to each investor
Investors own units of a pooled scheme rather than securities directly
Securities are held in each investor's own demat account
Each investor receives a separate, individually managed portfolio from the fund manager
In a mutual fund, money is pooled and investors hold units. In PMS, securities are held in each client's own name and the portfolio can be tailored.
REITs in India primarily invest in:
Unlisted start-up equity
Short-term government securities
Agricultural commodity futures
Income-generating commercial real estate
Real Estate Investment Trusts own rent-yielding properties such as offices and malls, and distribute most of their income to unitholders. InvITs do the same for infrastructure assets.
Exchange-traded funds differ from regular open-ended index funds mainly because ETFs:
Are always actively managed by star fund managers
Trade on stock exchanges at market prices during the day
Can only be bought from the AMC at end-of-day NAV
Are not regulated by SEBI
ETF units are listed and trade throughout the day like shares, at prices close to their indicative NAV. Index funds are bought and redeemed at end-of-day NAV through the AMC.
A client with ₹30 lakh wants professionally managed, diversified equity exposure. Which product is suitable given minimum investment rules?
A discretionary PMS account
A Category III AIF
An equity mutual fund scheme
A Category II private equity AIF
PMS requires a minimum of ₹50 lakh and AIFs generally ₹1 crore, so ₹30 lakh is too little for them. Equity mutual funds suit this client with low minimums and daily liquidity.
Which is a typical advantage of PMS over mutual funds for a high-net-worth client?
Lower minimum investment and lower costs than mutual funds in all cases
Portfolio customisation and direct ownership of securities
Guaranteed outperformance of mutual funds
Exemption from capital gains tax
PMS offers tailoring, concentrated portfolios and transparency at the security level. It often costs more, needs a large minimum and carries no guarantee of better returns.
Specialised Investment Funds (SIFs) introduced by SEBI are designed to:
Replace all PMS services from 2026
Fill the gap between mutual funds and PMS, with a higher minimum ticket
Offer guaranteed returns to retail investors
Invest only in unlisted real estate
SIFs are offered by eligible mutual funds under a separate brand, allow more flexible strategies than regular schemes, and have a higher minimum investment than mutual funds.
InvITs pay unitholders mainly from:
Profits from trading equity shares
Premiums collected on insurance policies
Interest on credit card loans
Cash flows from infrastructure assets such as roads or transmission lines
Infrastructure Investment Trusts own operating infrastructure and distribute much of the cash it generates, such as toll or transmission charges, to unitholders.
Which collective vehicle typically offers the highest transparency of daily portfolio value to retail investors?
A close-ended Category II AIF
A private real estate fund
An open-ended mutual fund with daily NAV
An unlisted venture capital fund
Open-ended mutual funds publish NAV every business day. Close-ended AIFs and private funds value holdings less frequently and report periodically to investors.

Role of Portfolio Managers.overview: This chapter explains who a portfolio manager is under SEBI (Portfolio Managers) Regulations, 2020, and the types of services offered: discretionary, non-discretionary and advisory. It covers the portfolio manager's duties as a fiduciary, the minimum investment per client, the client profile suited to PMS, the role of the principal officer and the distributor, and how PMS can be used for specific needs like concentrated equity, debt or multi-asset strategies. Know clearly who takes decisions in each service type and what the client should expect.
questions: Which of the following can offer portfolio management services to clients in India?
Any stock broker, without needing a separate registration, if clients agree
A chartered accountant who manages money for friends and relatives for a fee
A bank branch manager acting in a personal capacity outside the bank
An entity registered with SEBI as a portfolio manager

Managing client portfolios for consideration requires SEBI registration under the Portfolio Managers Regulations, 2020. A broker, accountant or banker cannot offer PMS without obtaining that registration.
Under SEBI rules, the minimum amount a client (other than an accredited investor) must invest in PMS is:
₹50 lakh, in funds or securities
₹25 lakh, in cash only
₹1 crore, in cash only
₹10 lakh, in funds or securities
The PMS minimum is ₹50 lakh, which may be brought in as funds, securities or a combination, valued as specified. Accredited investors may be exempted under the framework.
Who is responsible for the overall activities of a portfolio manager's business and is required to meet qualification and experience norms?
The custodian
The distributor
The client's chartered accountant
The principal officer
The principal officer is designated to be responsible for the PMS's decisions and functioning and must meet SEBI's qualification, experience and certification requirements.
A client wants a portfolio manager to manage her money but insists on approving every trade. Which service fits?
Discretionary portfolio management
Investment in a Category III AIF
Non-discretionary portfolio management
A passive index fund
Non-discretionary PMS keeps the client in control of decisions while the manager researches, recommends and executes. Discretionary PMS gives decision-making power to the manager.
As a fiduciary, a portfolio manager must:
Maximise its own fee income above all
Guarantee a minimum return every year
Place the client's interests above its own
Invest only in its group companies
Fiduciary duty means acting in good faith and in the client's best interest, avoiding or managing conflicts. It does not include guaranteeing returns.
A PMS distributor's main role is to:
Explain the PMS offering to suitable clients and facilitate onboarding
Take discretionary investment decisions for clients
Hold client securities in custody
Audit the portfolio manager's accounts
Distributors introduce clients to PMS, explain features, risks and costs, and help with paperwork. Investment decisions, custody and audit are handled by others.
Which client is generally most suited to a concentrated equity PMS strategy?
A high-net-worth investor with a long horizon and high risk capacity
A retiree who depends fully on the portfolio for regular monthly household expenses
A young investor with ₹5 lakh savings
A trust that needs capital safety within one year
Concentrated equity portfolios can be volatile. They suit wealthy, long-horizon investors who can absorb drawdowns, not those needing safety, income or small-ticket investing.
In an advisory PMS arrangement, the execution of trades is done by:
The portfolio manager without client consent
The stock exchange on the manager's instructions
The custodian on its own judgement
The client, based on advice received
Advisory services provide recommendations only. The client decides and executes, and the portfolio manager has no control over the account.

Operational Aspects of Portfolio Manager.overview: This chapter covers the operational framework for PMS: the disclosure document, client agreement, KYC and account opening, separate demat and bank accounts, custody, fees and charges (management fee, performance fee with high-water mark, operating expenses, exit load), periodic reporting, audits, direct onboarding without distributors, and closure of accounts. These rules exist to protect clients and ensure transparency, so focus on what must be disclosed and when, and how fees are calculated.
questions: Before signing a PMS agreement, the client must receive the portfolio manager's:
Annual tax return
Scheme information document
Red herring prospectus
Disclosure document
The disclosure document describes the manager, services, fees, risks, performance and conflicts. It must be provided to the client before the agreement is executed.
Under SEBI norms, a portfolio manager charges a performance fee on a high-water mark basis. This means the fee is charged:
On every positive return in a quarter
On the original investment amount every year, irrespective of the portfolio's returns
Only when the client redeems fully
Only on gains above the highest value the portfolio has previously reached
The high-water mark ensures clients do not pay performance fees for recovering past losses. Fees apply only to new gains above the previous peak value.
A client exits a PMS within the first year. Exit load, if charged, is capped by SEBI at:
1% of the amount redeemed
5% of the amount redeemed
10% of the amount redeemed
3% of the amount redeemed
SEBI caps PMS exit load at 3% in the first year, 2% in the second, 1% in the third, and nil thereafter. This prevents excessive penalties on exit.
Which of the following charges is NOT permitted to be collected from PMS clients?
Management fees
Performance fees
Upfront fees
Exit load within limits
SEBI prohibits portfolio managers from charging upfront fees directly or indirectly. Management fees, performance fees and capped exit loads are permitted with disclosure.
A client's PMS portfolio started the year at ₹60 lakh and ended at ₹69 lakh (no flows). With a 2% management fee on average assets of ₹64.5 lakh and no performance fee, the management fee is:
₹1.20 lakh
₹1.29 lakh
₹1.38 lakh
₹0.18 lakh
Management fee = 2% × ₹64.5 lakh = ₹1.29 lakh. Using opening or closing values would give a different number, so the agreement must specify the fee base.
PMS clients can come on board directly with a portfolio manager. The benefit of direct onboarding is that:
The client is exempt from the minimum investment
No distribution commission is charged to the client
The client is guaranteed better returns
The client need not sign an agreement
SEBI requires portfolio managers to offer direct onboarding without distributor involvement, so clients avoid distribution costs. All other requirements still apply.
Securities of each discretionary PMS client must be held:
In the portfolio manager's own proprietary demat account, along with its own investments
In a single pooled account shared by all clients
In a separate demat account in the client's name, with a custodian
In physical form with the distributor
Each client's securities are kept separately in the client's name and held through a custodian. This protects clients if the manager faces problems.
The portfolio manager must send each client periodic reports. These reports typically show:
Only the manager's marketing brochures
Personal details of other clients
Holdings, transactions, fees charged and portfolio performance
Only the stock market's index levels
Periodic reports provide transparency on what the client owns, trades done, expenses and fees debited, and returns. Other clients' data must never be shared.

Portfolio Management Process.overview: This chapter covers the step-by-step process of managing a client's portfolio: understanding the client (objectives, risk profile, constraints), drafting an investment policy, strategic and tactical asset allocation, security selection, execution, monitoring and rebalancing, and reviewing the plan as circumstances change. Constraints include liquidity, horizon, taxes, legal and regulatory factors and unique preferences. Questions often present a client scenario, so practise identifying which step or constraint is relevant.
questions: A client tells the portfolio manager she does not want to invest in tobacco or alcohol companies. In an investment policy, this is a:
Liquidity constraint
Time horizon constraint
Unique circumstance or preference constraint
Tax constraint
Ethical or personal restrictions are recorded as unique preferences. Liquidity, horizon and tax constraints relate to cash needs, time and tax status.
Tactical asset allocation differs from strategic allocation because it:
Sets the long-term policy mix of assets based on the client's goals and constraints
Never changes the asset weights once set
Is decided by the stock exchange
Makes short-term deviations to exploit perceived market opportunities
Strategic allocation is the long-term baseline. Tactical allocation tilts away from it temporarily to take advantage of market views, within agreed ranges.
A client's target is 70% equity and 30% debt. After a fall in equity, the mix is 60/40. Rebalancing would involve:
Selling more equity to reduce risk further
Holding the mix at 60/40 permanently
Selling some debt and buying equity
Moving everything into cash
Rebalancing restores the target by selling the overweight asset (debt) and buying the underweight one (equity). It enforces a disciplined 'buy low, sell high' approach.
Which is the best measure of a client's 'risk capacity'?
How excited she gets about stock tips
Her financial ability to absorb losses without affecting key goals
Her preference for well-known brands
The number of trading apps on her phone
Risk capacity is objective: income, wealth, liabilities and horizon. Risk tolerance is the psychological willingness to take risk. Suitability needs both.
Monitoring a PMS portfolio is necessary because:
Markets, client circumstances and goals change over time
The initial allocation is guaranteed to remain optimal for the client's whole life
SEBI forbids any change after account opening
Monitoring replaces the need for an investment policy
Investment management is a continuous loop. Changes in markets or the client's life — such as retirement or a new liability — may require revisiting the allocation.
A client aged 58 plans to retire in 2 years and will need regular income. The most appropriate change to his growth-oriented portfolio is to:
Gradually increase the allocation to stable income-generating assets
Shift entirely into small-cap stocks
Borrow to increase equity exposure
Ignore the coming retirement, since equity markets always rise over the long run
Approaching retirement shortens the horizon and raises income needs. A gradual shift toward income assets reduces sequence-of-returns risk while keeping some growth.
Which step usually comes first in the portfolio management process?
Selecting individual stocks
Measuring performance against benchmark
Understanding the client's objectives and constraints
Executing trades on the exchange
All later steps depend on knowing what the client wants and what limits apply. Security selection and execution follow the investment policy, and evaluation comes last.
An investor's liquidity constraint is best illustrated by:
A wish to beat the Nifty 50 every year
A preference for growth stocks over value stocks
Interest in global markets
A need to withdraw ₹15 lakh in 6 months for a home down-payment
Liquidity constraints arise from known or likely cash needs. The portion needed soon must be kept in liquid, low-volatility assets.

Performance Measurement and Evaluation o.overview: This chapter explains how PMS returns are calculated and compared. It covers holding period and annualised returns, time-weighted rate of return (TWRR) as mandated by SEBI, money-weighted returns, risk measures (standard deviation, beta, tracking error), risk-adjusted ratios (Sharpe, Treynor, Jensen's alpha, information ratio), and SEBI's standardised benchmarking framework for PMS strategies. Practise calculations and understand why TWRR removes the effect of client cash flows.
questions: SEBI requires portfolio managers to report performance using TWRR mainly because it:
Always shows higher returns than other methods, which makes the manager look better
Removes the effect of client deposits and withdrawals on returns
Includes the client's tax payments in returns
Is easier to compute without any data
TWRR links returns of sub-periods between cash flows, so the manager is judged on investment decisions, not on when clients added or withdrew money.
A portfolio returned +20% in year 1 and −10% in year 2. Its cumulative return over two years is:
Cumulative return = 1.20 × 0.90 − 1 = 1.08 − 1 = 8%. Simply adding gives 10%, which overstates the result because losses apply to a larger base.
A portfolio earned 15% with beta 0.9. The risk-free rate is 6% and the market returned 14%. Jensen's alpha is:
CAPM expected = 6 + 0.9 × (14 − 6) = 6 + 7.2 = 13.2%. Alpha = 15 − 13.2 = 1.8%. A positive alpha indicates return above what the portfolio's beta would justify.
Under SEBI's PMS benchmarking framework, the benchmark for each strategy is chosen from:
Any index the manager prefers, selected after the year ends based on relative performance
The best-performing mutual fund of the year
A set of benchmarks prescribed for the strategy's broad investment approach
The repo rate set by the RBI
SEBI requires managers to choose a Tier-1 benchmark linked to the strategy's investment approach (equity, debt, hybrid or multi-asset) so clients can compare strategies consistently.
Two PMS strategies earned 18%. Strategy P had standard deviation 15% and Q had 20%; the risk-free rate is 6%. Which is better on the Sharpe ratio?
Q, with Sharpe 0.90 against 0.80
Both are equal at 1.20
P, with Sharpe 0.80 against 0.60
Q, because higher risk deserves preference
Sharpe P = (18 − 6) / 15 = 0.80; Sharpe Q = (18 − 6) / 20 = 0.60. With equal returns, the strategy with lower volatility delivers more return per unit of total risk.
Tracking error of a portfolio measures:
The number of trading errors made by the manager
The variability of its returns relative to its benchmark
The difference between gross and net returns
The total return over one year
Tracking error is the standard deviation of the difference between portfolio and benchmark returns. Higher tracking error means the portfolio deviates more from its benchmark.
Which measure is most appropriate when a PMS portfolio is only a small part of a client's well-diversified wealth?
Sharpe ratio
Maximum drawdown alone
Treynor ratio
Dividend yield
If the client is already diversified, only the portfolio's systematic risk matters, measured by beta. Treynor divides excess return by beta, making it suitable here.
A distributor shows a client only the best-performing PMS account of a manager. This is misleading because:
Performance should reflect the strategy's overall results, not selected accounts
Best performance by one account is always repeated by all other accounts in the future
Individual accounts cannot be measured
SEBI forbids any mention of returns

Cherry-picking the best account hides the real experience of most clients of that strategy. SEBI requires strategy-level performance reporting so that prospective clients see representative, comparable results.

Taxation.overview: This chapter explains the tax treatment of investments held through PMS. Since securities are held in the client's name, each transaction is taxed in the client's hands: short-term and long-term capital gains on listed equity, debt instruments and mutual fund units, dividend income, interest income, STT, and the treatment of PMS fees. It also covers set-off and carry-forward of losses and tax issues for non-resident clients. Tax rates change with Budgets, so learn the principles and confirm current rates before advising.
questions: In PMS, capital gains from each sale in a client's portfolio are taxed:
At the portfolio manager's level as a business
Only when the client closes the account
In the client's own hands, transaction by transaction
At a flat rate on the total portfolio value
The client owns the securities directly, so each sale creates a gain or loss for the client in the year of sale. This differs from a mutual fund, where tax arises on redemption of units.
Listed equity shares held for more than 12 months and sold by a PMS client generate:
Short-term capital gains
Business income in all cases
Income from other sources
Long-term capital gains
For listed equity shares, the holding period threshold for long-term status is 12 months. Gains on shares held for 12 months or less are short-term.
A PMS client books a short-term capital loss on listed shares. Under tax rules, this loss can be set off against:
Salary income only
Short-term or long-term capital gains
Rental income only
Only long-term gains in the same year
Short-term capital losses can be set off against both short- and long-term capital gains, and unused losses may be carried forward for up to eight years if the return is filed on time.
A PMS client books a long-term capital loss on sale of listed shares. Under tax rules, this loss can be set off against:
Short-term capital gains as well as salary income in the same year
Only long-term capital gains
Any income, including business and rental income, in the same year
Only short-term capital gains arising from debt mutual funds

Long-term capital losses can be set off only against long-term capital gains, and unused losses can be carried forward for up to eight years. Short-term losses, by contrast, can be set off against both types of gains.
Frequent churning in a PMS portfolio matters for taxes mainly because it:
Reduces the client's tax rate to zero
Creates more short-term gains, which may be taxed at higher rates
Converts all gains into exempt income
Has no tax impact for PMS clients
High turnover realises gains sooner and often as short-term gains, which are taxed at higher rates than long-term equity gains. Post-tax returns can fall sharply.
A non-resident Indian investing through PMS should note that:
NRIs are fully exempt from Indian capital gains tax on listed shares held through PMS
NRIs cannot invest in Indian PMS at all
Gains are taxed only in the PMS manager's hands
Tax may be deducted at source on capital gains, subject to treaty relief
For NRIs, tax is generally withheld at source on capital gains. They may claim relief under applicable tax treaties by providing the required documents.
Securities Transaction Tax (STT) in a PMS account is:
A tax on the PMS management fee
Paid on exchange transactions in equity and equity derivatives
A refundable deposit collected by SEBI
Charged only on government bonds
STT is collected by the exchange on specified transactions such as sale and purchase of listed equity and derivatives. It forms part of transaction costs.
Why should a PMS distributor avoid giving precise tax rate assurances to clients?
Tax rates and rules change with Budgets and individual situations differ
Because PMS clients never pay tax
Because SEBI fixes tax rates every month
Because taxes do not affect the net returns that PMS clients finally receive
Tax laws are amended frequently, and the outcome depends on the client's residency, income and holding periods. Clients should verify current rules with a tax professional.

Regulatory, Governance and Ethical Aspec.overview: This chapter covers SEBI (Portfolio Managers) Regulations, 2020 and related circulars: registration and net worth requirements, principal officer and compliance officer, code of conduct, conflict of interest, restrictions on investment in associates and unlisted securities, prevention of mis-selling, distributor obligations, grievance redressal through SCORES and online dispute resolution, and penalties. It also covers ethical selling: suitability, disclosure of commissions, no assurance of returns and fair treatment. Expect scenario questions on what a distributor should or should not do.
questions: A PMS distributor promises a client that the strategy 'cannot fall more than 5%'. This is:
Acceptable if the past three years support it
Misleading, since no market-linked strategy can assure limits on losses
Required disclosure under SEBI rules
Permitted, as long as the client is a high-net-worth individual who understands markets
Assuring returns or limits on losses misrepresents risk. Distributors must give balanced information and not promise outcomes that depend on markets.
A PMS distributor receives commission from the portfolio manager. SEBI expects this commission to be:
Kept confidential from the client
Disclosed to the client and paid on a trail basis
Paid fully upfront at account opening
Deducted directly from the client's capital without disclosure
Distributors must disclose all commissions to clients, and SEBI requires trail-based payment, discouraging churning and mis-selling driven by upfront payouts.
An investor's complaint against a portfolio manager remains unresolved. The investor can next approach:
SEBI's SCORES platform, and then online dispute resolution if needed
The RBI Banking Ombudsman
The local police station only
The stock exchange's listing department
SEBI-registered intermediaries are covered by SCORES, and further escalation is possible through the online dispute resolution (ODR) mechanism. The banking ombudsman covers banks.
A distributor recommends a high-risk small-cap PMS strategy to a 72-year-old client needing steady income, because it pays higher commission. This is primarily:
Mis-selling that breaches the suitability obligation
Acceptable, because the client has already read and signed the PMS agreement
Good practice since small caps have high returns
A tax planning strategy
Recommendations must match the client's profile. Pushing an unsuitable product for higher commission is mis-selling, regardless of the client's signature.
Which certification must individuals distributing PMS products generally hold?
NISM Series XXI-A certification
NISM Series V-A only
An IRDAI insurance agent licence
A CA qualification
SEBI requires PMS distributors and their employees engaged in selling PMS to hold NISM Series XXI-A (Portfolio Management Services Distributors) certification.
A portfolio manager invests a client's funds in securities of its own associate companies. SEBI requires:
No limits at all, as long as the manager genuinely believes in the associate company's stock
A ban on any investment in listed companies
Only the distributor's approval
Compliance with specified limits and prior client consent
Investing in associates creates a conflict of interest. SEBI caps such exposure and requires client consent and disclosure to protect clients.
Apart from the principal officer, SEBI requires a portfolio manager to appoint which official to monitor adherence to regulations and report non-compliance?
An independent statutory auditor nominated by the distributor
A client representative elected by all PMS investors
A depository participant appointed for each client account
A compliance officer
Portfolio managers must appoint a compliance officer, separate from the principal officer, who monitors compliance with the Act, regulations and circulars and reports any non-compliance to SEBI.
A distributor shares a client's portfolio statement with another prospect to show 'how well clients are doing'. This breaches:
Exit load rules
Minimum investment rules
Client confidentiality
Net worth requirements
Client information must be kept confidential and used only for the client's service. Showing it to others without consent breaches the code of conduct and data protection norms.

Investment Landscape.overview: This chapter gives the portfolio manager's view of the Indian investment landscape: household savings and their shift towards financial assets, the main asset classes (equity, fixed income, real estate, gold, cash and alternatives), the role of financial intermediaries and the range of investment products available. It also introduces the concepts of risk, return, liquidity, inflation and the investor life cycle. Focus on how different investor segments use different products and why portfolio management services fit high-net-worth investors with specific needs.
questions: Over the long run, the main reason an investor accepts equity volatility is:
Equity prices are protected by SEBI against falls of more than 10% a year
Equity dividends are fixed in advance like bank deposit interest
The potential to earn returns above inflation
Equity markets in India never fall over any three-year period
Equity offers ownership in growing businesses, giving potential returns above inflation over long periods. Prices are not protected, dividends are not fixed and multi-year losses can occur.
An investor in the 'accumulation' phase of the life cycle typically:
Draws down savings to meet everyday living expenses after retirement
Transfers wealth to heirs through wills and trusts as the main priority
Builds wealth with a long horizon and steady income
Holds almost all wealth in cash because no goals remain
The accumulation phase covers working years, when income exceeds spending and the horizon is long, allowing more growth assets. Drawing down and wealth transfer belong to later stages.
Which asset class generally offers the highest liquidity with the lowest price risk?
Cash and short-term money-market instruments
Unlisted shares of a private company in a growing sector
A commercial office property in a metro city
Listed small-cap equity shares with low trading volume
Cash and money-market instruments can be converted quickly with little change in value. Unlisted shares, property and thinly traded small caps are slow or costly to sell.
Financialisation of household savings in India refers to:
A shift from mutual funds back to gold jewellery and land
The government taking control of all household bank deposits
A shift from physical assets to financial assets
Banks converting savings accounts into fixed deposits automatically

Indian households have traditionally held much wealth in gold and real estate. Financialisation describes the growing share of savings going into deposits, mutual funds, equities, insurance and pensions.
An investor's nominal portfolio return is 10% and inflation is 6.5%. The approximate real return is:
Approximate real return = nominal return − inflation = 10 − 6.5 = 3.5%. The exact figure is 1.10 / 1.065 − 1 ≈ 3.3%, slightly lower than the approximation.
Which product would generally NOT be considered a market-linked investment?
A bank fixed deposit
An equity-oriented mutual fund scheme bought through SIP
Units of a listed REIT traded on the exchange
A discretionary PMS equity strategy
A fixed deposit pays a contracted rate regardless of market movement. Mutual fund units, REIT units and PMS portfolios fluctuate with market prices.
A high-net-worth investor chooses PMS over a mutual fund mainly to obtain:
A guaranteed return that is higher than any mutual fund scheme can offer
A customised portfolio held in her own name
Exemption from all taxes on capital gains made in the portfolio
The ability to invest with a ticket size of just ₹5,000
PMS offers individual portfolios, direct ownership and tailoring to the client's needs. It carries no guarantee, no tax exemption and requires a minimum of ₹50 lakh.
Liquidity risk for an investor means the risk that:
The company issuing the asset will stop all business operations
An asset cannot be sold quickly without a price concession
Inflation will be higher than the return on the asset
Interest rates will fall after the asset is bought
Liquidity risk concerns the ability to convert an asset to cash at a fair price when needed. Business failure is credit or business risk; inflation and rate changes are separate risks.

Introduction to Securities Markets.overview: This chapter explains how Indian securities markets work from a portfolio manager's perspective: primary and secondary markets, market participants and intermediaries, trading mechanisms, order types, clearing and settlement, depositories, and the regulatory role of SEBI, RBI and the Ministry of Finance. It also covers market indices, market capitalisation segments and investor protection measures. Understand how trades are executed and settled for client portfolios and what each intermediary is responsible for.
questions: A 'stop-loss' sell order is generally used to:
Buy more shares automatically whenever the price rises by a set amount
Guarantee that shares are sold at exactly the trigger price in all conditions
Limit losses if the price falls to a trigger level
Cancel all pending orders at the end of the trading day
A stop-loss order becomes active when the trigger price is hit and then sells, limiting further losses. In fast markets it may execute below the trigger, so the price is not guaranteed.
Which market segment is used by the Reserve Bank of India to conduct auctions of Government securities?
The primary market for G-secs
The equity cash segment of a stock exchange
The commodity derivatives segment of an exchange
The SME platform of a stock exchange
The RBI issues G-secs on behalf of the government through primary auctions. Secondary trading happens on platforms like NDS-OM and exchange debt segments.
Novation by a clearing corporation means it:
Becomes the counterparty to both buyer and seller
Chooses which brokers are allowed to trade on a particular day
Transfers shares directly from the company to the buyer
Sets the issue price for initial public offerings
Novation replaces the original contract between buyer and seller with two contracts with the clearing corporation, which removes counterparty risk between trading members.
Shares of a listed company that are pledged by promoters are a concern to portfolio managers mainly because:
Pledged shares cannot be counted in the company's market capitalisation at all
SEBI bans the company from paying dividends while any pledge exists
Pledged shares automatically convert into debt of the company
Forced selling by lenders can hit the share price
If the share price falls, lenders may invoke the pledge and sell, adding to downward pressure. High promoter pledging is a governance and risk signal analysts watch.
Which of the following is regulated primarily by the RBI rather than SEBI?
Stock brokers in the equity cash segment
The government securities and money markets
Mutual funds and their asset management companies
Portfolio managers registered under the 2020 Regulations
RBI regulates the G-sec, money and foreign exchange markets, along with banks and NBFCs. Brokers, mutual funds and portfolio managers are regulated by SEBI.
An investor sees a stock's 'circuit filter' hit on the upper side. This means:
The stock has been permanently delisted from the stock exchange
The company has announced a bonus issue for all shareholders
Trading is restricted beyond a set price band for the day
The stock's price is guaranteed to rise further the next day
Price bands limit how far a stock can move in a day to curb volatility. Once the band is hit, trades cannot happen beyond it until the next session or band revision.
The market capitalisation category of a stock for Indian mutual funds and many portfolio managers is based on:
The number of shareholders recorded in the company's register
The face value of its shares and the size of its dividend
Its ranking by full market capitalisation in AMFI's list
The number of employees it has across all its offices
AMFI publishes a half-yearly list ranking companies by full market cap: 1–100 large cap, 101–250 mid cap and the rest small cap. The industry widely uses this classification.
Which document must a company file for an IPO that gives investors detailed information about the issue?
The offer document or prospectus
The portfolio manager's disclosure document for its PMS clients
The company's annual GST return filed with the tax department
The depository's statement of holdings for promoters
Issuers disclose business, financials, risks and issue terms through the draft and final offer documents filed with SEBI and the exchanges. Investors should read them before applying.

Investing in Stocks.overview: This chapter covers equity research and valuation for portfolio managers. It explains top-down and bottom-up approaches, economy and industry analysis, company analysis using financial statements, key ratios (ROE, ROCE, margins, leverage, turnover), valuation through discounted cash flow, dividend discount and relative multiples (P/E, P/B, EV/EBITDA), and an introduction to technical analysis. Practise calculations such as the Gordon growth model, sustainable growth and EV/EBITDA, and learn which method suits which kind of company.
questions: A company is expected to pay a dividend of ₹6 next year, growing at 8% forever. If the required return is 14%, its value per share under the Gordon growth model is:
Value = D1 / (r − g) = 6 / (0.14 − 0.08) = 6 / 0.06 = ₹100. The model works only when the required return exceeds the growth rate.
Enterprise value (EV) of a company is generally calculated as:
Market cap − debt + cash and cash equivalents held
Market cap + debt − cash
Book value of equity + reserves − all current liabilities
Net profit × dividend payout ratio × number of shares
EV measures the value of the whole business to all capital providers. Debt is added because an acquirer must pay it off, and cash is subtracted because it reduces the net cost.
A company has EV of ₹1,200 crore and EBITDA of ₹150 crore. Its EV/EBITDA multiple is:
EV/EBITDA = 1,200 ÷ 150 = 8. This multiple is useful for comparing companies with different capital structures, because EV includes debt and EBITDA is before interest.
Return on capital employed (ROCE) differs from ROE mainly because ROCE:
Uses net profit after tax divided only by shareholders' equity
Ignores debt and measures only the dividend paid per share
Is calculated only for banks and insurance companies
Uses operating profit on equity plus debt
ROCE = EBIT ÷ (equity + debt), showing returns on all capital in the business. ROE uses net profit on equity only and can be inflated by leverage.
A bottom-up stock selection approach begins with:
A forecast of GDP growth, inflation and interest rates for the economy
Choosing the best-performing sectors for the next two years first
Selecting a benchmark index and copying its weights exactly
Analysis of individual companies
Bottom-up investors focus on company fundamentals first, regardless of economic or sector views. Top-down investing starts from the economy and then narrows to sectors and stocks.
A firm's ROE is 18% and it pays out 40% of earnings as dividends. Its sustainable growth rate is approximately:
Sustainable growth = ROE × retention ratio = 18% × (1 − 0.40) = 18% × 0.60 = 10.8%. Retained earnings reinvested at the ROE drive growth without new equity.
A discounted cash flow (DCF) valuation is most sensitive to:
The discount rate and terminal growth assumptions
The company's face value per share and its listing date
The number of shareholders who attended the last AGM
The colour and design of the company's annual report
Most DCF value often lies in the terminal value, which depends heavily on long-term growth and the discount rate. Small changes in these inputs can change the valuation substantially.
A 'moving average crossover' signal is a tool of:
Technical analysis
Fundamental analysis of the company's balance sheet and cash flows
Credit analysis of the company's bonds by rating agencies
Macroeconomic analysis of the country's current account
Technical analysts use price-based indicators such as moving averages; a short-term average crossing above a long-term one is read as bullish. Fundamental analysis studies business value.

Investing in Fixed Income Securities.overview: This chapter covers bond investing for portfolio managers: bond features and types, pricing and yield measures (current yield, YTM, yield to call), the term structure and yield curve shapes, duration, modified duration and convexity, credit risk, ratings and spreads, and the Indian debt market segments such as G-secs, SDLs, corporate bonds, CPs and CDs. Practise bond pricing and duration-based price change calculations and understand how yield curve changes affect different bonds.
questions: A bond with face value ₹1,000 and coupon 8% is trading at ₹1,050. Which statement is correct?
Its YTM is below 8%
Its YTM is above 8% because the price is above face value
Its current yield equals its coupon rate of exactly 8%
It is trading at a discount to its face value
A bond priced above face value is at a premium, so the buyer gets less than the coupon rate as yield. Current yield = 80 ÷ 1,050 ≈ 7.6%, also below 8%.
An upward-sloping (normal) yield curve indicates that:
Short-term yields are higher than long-term yields for all maturities
All maturities offer exactly the same yield to investors
Long-term yields are higher than short-term yields
Bond prices are guaranteed to rise over the next year
A normal yield curve slopes upward because investors usually demand extra yield for longer maturities. An inverted curve, with short yields above long yields, often signals slowing growth.
Convexity is valuable to a bond investor because, for large yield changes, it means:
Prices fall more and rise less than duration alone would suggest
The bond's coupon automatically resets to market rates
The bond becomes free of all credit and liquidity risk
Prices rise more and fall less than duration predicts
Duration is a linear estimate. Positive convexity curves the price–yield line so actual gains exceed and losses fall short of the duration estimate for big moves.
A bond has modified duration 6 and convexity effects can be ignored. If its yield rises from 7.0% to 7.5%, its price changes by approximately:
Price change ≈ −modified duration × change in yield = −6 × 0.5% = −3%. Prices move opposite to yields, scaled by duration.
A callable bond is less attractive to investors than a similar non-callable bond because:
The investor must hold it until maturity without any coupon payments
It always carries a lower credit rating than non-callable bonds
Its coupons are taxed at a higher rate than other bonds
The issuer may redeem it early when rates fall
Issuers call bonds when rates fall, forcing investors to reinvest at lower yields and capping price gains. Investors therefore demand a higher yield for callable bonds.
State Development Loans (SDLs) are bonds issued by:
State governments
Public sector banks for funding home loans to individuals
The Central Government to fund the Union budget deficit
Municipal corporations to fund local water projects only
SDLs are market borrowings of state governments, auctioned through the RBI. They usually yield slightly more than Central Government securities of similar maturity.
The credit spread on a corporate bond is the:
Difference between the bond's coupon and the RBI repo rate
Brokerage paid when buying the bond in the secondary market
Gap between the bond's face value and its issue price
Extra yield over a comparable government bond
Credit spread compensates for default and liquidity risk relative to a risk-free G-sec of similar maturity. Spreads widen when credit risk is perceived to rise.
A zero-coupon bond's Macaulay duration is:
Equal to its time to maturity
Always zero, because it does not pay any coupon at all
Half of its time to maturity in all cases
Longer than its time to maturity
A zero-coupon bond pays a single cash flow at maturity, so its weighted average time to cash flow equals its maturity. Coupon bonds have durations shorter than maturity.

Derivatives.overview: This chapter explains how portfolio managers use derivatives: futures and options on indices and stocks, pricing through cost of carry, option pay-offs and basic strategies (protective put, covered call, collar, spreads), the option Greeks at an introductory level, and hedging with beta-adjusted futures. It also covers margins, mark-to-market and SEBI's limits on derivatives use in PMS. Practise hedge-ratio and pay-off calculations and understand when derivatives reduce versus add risk.
questions: A portfolio worth ₹5 crore has a beta of 0.8. The Nifty futures contract value is ₹20 lakh. The number of contracts to sell for a full hedge is:
Hedge value = portfolio × beta = ₹5 crore × 0.8 = ₹4 crore. Contracts = ₹4 crore ÷ ₹20 lakh = 20. Ignoring beta would suggest 25 contracts, over-hedging the portfolio.
A covered call strategy involves:
Buying a call option without owning the underlying shares
Holding a stock and selling a call on it
Selling a put option and holding cash to cover assignment
Buying both a call and a put at the same strike price
The investor owns the shares and writes calls against them to earn premium, accepting a cap on upside. Buying a call and put together is a straddle.
An option's delta of 0.6 means that, for a small ₹1 rise in the underlying price, the option premium will change by about:
Delta measures the sensitivity of the option price to the underlying. A delta of 0.6 implies about ₹0.60 change for a ₹1 move in the underlying, for small changes.
A 'collar' on a stock holding is created by:
Selling a put and buying a call on the stock at the same strike
Buying futures and simultaneously buying a call option
Selling the stock and buying a government bond with the proceeds
Buying a put and selling a call on the stock
A collar buys downside protection (put) and funds it partly by selling upside (call). The result is a range of outcomes bounded on both sides.
Option theta measures:
Loss of option value as time passes
The change in option price for a change in interest rates
The change in delta for a change in the underlying price
The change in option price for a change in volatility
Theta captures time decay — options lose value as expiry nears, all else equal. Rho relates to interest rates, gamma to changes in delta and vega to volatility.
A portfolio manager expects a stock to stay in a narrow range until expiry. Which strategy best fits this view?
Selling a strangle
Buying a straddle at the current market price
Buying out-of-the-money call options only
Buying the stock's futures with full leverage

Selling out-of-the-money call and put options earns premium if the stock stays within the range. Buying a straddle profits from big moves, the opposite view. Short strangles carry large risk if the range breaks.
Initial margin on a futures position is meant to:
Pay the full contract value upfront to the seller
Cover potential one-day losses on the position
Act as brokerage paid to the trading member
Provide a guaranteed return on the investor's capital
Initial margin is collateral sized to cover likely adverse moves, typically based on risk models. Futures require only a fraction of the contract value, which creates leverage.
Vega of an option is highest for options that are:
At the money with longer time to expiry
Deep in the money and expiring the same day
Deep out of the money and expiring the same day
Already exercised by the buyer
Vega measures sensitivity to volatility. At-the-money options with more time remaining have the most time value and therefore respond most to changes in volatility.

Mutual Fund.overview: This chapter covers mutual funds as a comparison and complement to PMS. Topics include the three-tier structure (sponsor, trustee, AMC), types of schemes under SEBI categorisation, NAV computation, expense ratio and loads, direct and regular plans, systematic plans (SIP, SWP, STP), riskometer, scheme documents, and taxation of mutual fund units. Portfolio managers should understand how mutual fund costs, liquidity and regulation compare with PMS when advising clients.
questions: In India, the entity that holds mutual fund assets in trust for unitholders is the:
Board of trustees or trustee company
Asset management company that runs the investment portfolio
Registrar and transfer agent that maintains investor records
Stock exchange where the fund's trades are executed
Mutual funds are set up as trusts. Trustees hold assets for unitholders and oversee the AMC, which manages the money. RTAs and exchanges provide services but do not own assets.
A scheme's total expense ratio (TER) is charged:
Daily, through a reduction in NAV
Once a year as a separate invoice sent to each investor
Only at the time of redemption as a lump sum
Only on investors who invest through distributors
TER is accrued daily and deducted from scheme assets, so the NAV reflects it. It applies to all investors in a plan; direct plans have a lower TER than regular plans.
A Systematic Withdrawal Plan (SWP) is most useful for an investor who wants to:
Invest a fixed amount every month from salary into equity schemes
Shift money from a debt scheme to an equity scheme in instalments
Receive regular cash flows from investments
Lock in money for three years for tax benefits under the scheme
SWP redeems units periodically to provide regular income. SIP invests regularly, STP transfers between schemes and ELSS carries a lock-in.
Under SEBI's scheme categorisation, a flexi-cap fund must invest at least:
25% each in large, mid and small-cap stocks at all times
80% in large-cap stocks and the rest in debt
65% in equity across market caps
100% in mid-cap and small-cap stocks only
Flexi-cap funds must keep at least 65% in equity with freedom across market caps. Multi-cap funds, in contrast, must hold at least 25% each in large, mid and small caps.
A key difference between a mutual fund and a PMS for the investor is that, in a mutual fund:
Each trade made by the fund manager is taxed in the investor's hands
Tax arises only when the investor redeems units
The investor's minimum investment is ₹50 lakh in all cases
The investor can instruct the fund manager on which stocks to buy
Mutual fund trades inside the scheme do not create tax for unitholders; tax arises on redemption or transfer of units. In PMS, each sale is taxed in the client's hands.
An investor puts ₹12,000 into a scheme at NAV ₹40 and redeems all units when NAV is ₹46, with no loads. The absolute return is:
Units = 12,000 ÷ 40 = 300. Redemption value = 300 × 46 = ₹13,800. Absolute return = 1,800 ÷ 12,000 = 15%, the same as (46 − 40) ÷ 40.
The riskometer of a mutual fund scheme is:
Fixed at launch and never changed for the life of the scheme
Decided each year by the investors through a vote
Reviewed monthly based on the scheme's portfolio
Shown only to institutional investors and not to retail investors
SEBI requires AMCs to evaluate the riskometer monthly using portfolio-based parameters and disclose it, so investors can see changes in scheme risk.
Which mutual fund category is designed to track an index with minimal deviation?
Focused funds holding up to 30 high-conviction stocks
Contra funds that buy out-of-favour sectors
Dynamic asset allocation funds changing equity exposure
Index funds and ETFs
Passive funds replicate an index, aiming for low tracking error and low costs. Focused, contra and dynamic funds are actively managed.

Role of Portfolio Managers.overview: This chapter explains the role and responsibilities of portfolio managers under the SEBI (Portfolio Managers) Regulations, 2020. It covers the types of PMS services, the minimum investment, client eligibility including accredited investors, the qualifications and certification of the principal officer and key staff, the manager's fiduciary and suitability obligations, and how PMS strategies are designed and offered. Know clearly the distinctions between discretionary, non-discretionary and advisory mandates and what each implies for decision-making and liability.
questions: A portfolio manager registered with SEBI can accept as a client:
Only resident individuals, never companies, trusts or NRIs
Only investors who already hold a mutual fund account
Only investors recommended by a stock exchange
Any eligible investor meeting PMS norms
PMS is open to individuals, HUFs, companies, trusts, NRIs and others who meet KYC and minimum investment norms. There is no requirement to hold mutual funds or be referred by an exchange.
Accredited investors in PMS may be offered:
Lower minimums under the large value framework
Guaranteed returns linked to the repo rate
Exemption from KYC and anti-money laundering checks
Permission to use unlimited leverage on their accounts

SEBI allows portfolio managers to offer accredited investors flexibilities such as relaxation of the ₹50 lakh minimum under the large value accredited investor framework. KYC and leverage rules still apply.
In a discretionary PMS, who decides which securities to buy and sell?
The client, who must approve every single trade in advance
The portfolio manager, within the agreement
The custodian, based on its own market view
The distributor who introduced the client to the manager
Under a discretionary mandate, the client gives the manager authority to take investment decisions within the agreed objectives and restrictions. The custodian and distributor do not decide trades.
Under the 2020 Regulations, the principal officer of a portfolio manager must have:
Only a degree in any discipline without any work experience
Required qualification, experience and NISM certification
At least 25 years of experience as a stock broker
A licence from the Reserve Bank of India
SEBI specifies minimum professional qualifications, relevant experience and NISM certification for the principal officer, who is responsible for investment decisions and operations.
A portfolio manager's 'suitability' obligation requires it to:
Offer every client the strategy with the highest past return
Accept any client who meets the minimum investment, whatever their needs
Ensure that no client portfolio ever shows a loss
Match strategies to the client's risk profile and goals
Suitability means recommending only what fits the client's financial situation, risk tolerance and objectives. Past returns or minimum eligibility alone do not make a product suitable.
Which activity falls outside the scope of a portfolio manager's services?
Managing a client's equity portfolio on a discretionary basis
Advising a client on securities under an advisory mandate
Executing trades for a client after approval under non-discretionary PMS
Accepting deposits from clients with a fixed interest rate
Portfolio managers manage or advise on securities portfolios. Accepting deposits at fixed interest is a banking or NBFC activity and is not permitted for portfolio managers.
Employees of a portfolio manager involved in investment decision-making are required to:
Hold a separate SEBI registration as research analysts in all cases
Also register with IRDAI as insurance agents
Obtain the specified NISM certification
Have at least 15 years of experience in banking
SEBI requires the principal officer and employees in decision-making roles to hold the relevant NISM certification (Series XXI-B) to ensure minimum knowledge standards.
A client asks a discretionary portfolio manager to avoid all stocks in the alcohol sector. The manager should:
Ignore it, because discretionary managers decide everything freely
Refuse to accept the client because restrictions are not allowed
Move the client to a mutual fund without explaining why
Record the restriction and follow it
Discretionary authority operates within the client agreement. Client-specific restrictions should be documented and followed, as customisation is a key feature of PMS.

Operational Aspects of Portfolio Manager.overview: This chapter covers day-to-day operations of PMS: client onboarding, KYC and agreement, the disclosure document, custodian and bank account arrangements, trade execution and allocation, fee and expense computation, high-water mark mechanics, periodic statements and annual audit, handling of corporate actions, and closure or transfer of accounts. Practise fee computations with high-water marks and hurdle rates, and know what information clients must receive and how often.
questions: A client's portfolio is ₹1.20 crore at the end of year 1 (high-water mark) and ₹1.10 crore at the end of year 2. A 20% performance fee over the high-water mark in year 2 is:
₹2 lakh
₹4 lakh
Nil
₹22 lakh
The year-2 value is below the high-water mark of ₹1.20 crore, so no new gains exist and no performance fee is payable. Fees resume only after the portfolio exceeds ₹1.20 crore.
Portfolio managers must get each client's portfolio and accounts audited:
Only when the client asks for an audit in writing
Annually by an independent chartered accountant
Once every five years by the stock exchange
Daily by the client's distributor
SEBI requires annual audit of client accounts by an independent chartered accountant, with a copy of the certificate given to the client. This independently verifies holdings and fees.
Operating expenses charged to a PMS client, excluding brokerage, are:
Unlimited, provided they are mentioned somewhere in the agreement
Capped by SEBI as a percentage of average AUM
Paid fully by the distributor, never by the client
Charged only when the client's portfolio makes a loss
SEBI caps operating expenses (excluding brokerage) as a percentage of the client's average daily AUM. This prevents managers from loading clients with unlimited costs.
A PMS client wants to close the account and receive her securities instead of cash. The portfolio manager should:
Insist on selling all securities and paying only cash
Transfer the securities to her own demat account
Hold the securities until the next financial year
Transfer the securities to the distributor's account
Clients may choose to receive securities in specie on closure. The manager must arrange transfer to the client's own demat account after settling dues as per the agreement.
When the PM buys a stock for many discretionary clients in one block order, the shares must be allocated:
First to clients who pay the highest management fees
Only to the client accounts of the PM's own employees
Fairly as per a pre-defined allocation policy
Randomly, without keeping any records of the allocation
Block trades must be allocated according to a documented fair-allocation policy with records. Favouring higher-fee or related accounts is a conflict of interest.
A portfolio of ₹80 lakh grows to ₹96 lakh. The hurdle rate is 10% and the performance fee is 20% of returns above the hurdle (no catch-up). The performance fee is:
₹1.6 lakh
₹3.2 lakh
₹0.8 lakh
₹1.92 lakh
Hurdle value = 80 × 1.10 = ₹88 lakh. Excess = 96 − 88 = ₹8 lakh. Fee = 20% × 8 = ₹1.6 lakh. Charging 20% on the full ₹16 lakh gain would give ₹3.2 lakh.
Corporate actions such as dividends and bonus shares on PMS holdings are:
Credited to the respective client's account
Kept by the portfolio manager as part of its fee income
Shared equally among all clients regardless of holdings
Ignored because PMS accounts do not receive corporate actions
Since securities are held in each client's name, dividends, bonuses and other benefits accrue to that client. The manager must reflect them in client statements.
Before a portfolio manager changes the fee structure for an existing client, it should:
Simply deduct the new fees from the next quarter onwards
Inform only the distributor, who will tell the client later
Publish the change on its website and assume consent
Obtain the client's consent and amend the agreement
Fees are part of the client agreement, so changes require the client's informed consent. Deducting revised fees without agreement breaches the contract and SEBI norms.

Portfolio Management Process.overview: This chapter covers the full process of managing client portfolios: gathering client information, assessing risk tolerance and capacity, setting return objectives, identifying constraints (liquidity, horizon, tax, legal, unique), drafting an investment policy statement, strategic and tactical asset allocation, security selection, execution, monitoring and feedback. It also discusses goal-based investing and the role of behavioural factors in client communication. Expect case-based questions applying the process to different client profiles.
questions: A client requires a 9% annual return to meet her retirement goal but has low risk tolerance. The portfolio manager should first:
Invest aggressively to reach 9% regardless of her low tolerance
Promise her 9% so she remains comfortable with the plan
Discuss trade-offs and possibly revise the goal
Ignore her risk tolerance because the goal is more important
When required return and risk tolerance conflict, the manager must explain the trade-offs: save more, extend the horizon or lower the target. Ignoring tolerance or promising returns is unsuitable.
An investment policy statement (IPS) is most useful for:
Replacing the need for any client agreement with the manager
Guaranteeing that the portfolio will meet its target return
Allowing the manager to change the strategy without client input
Guiding decisions and evaluating the manager
The IPS documents objectives, constraints and allocation, giving a reference for decisions and reviews. It does not guarantee returns or replace legal agreements.
A 45-year-old client in the 30% tax bracket asks how taxes affect asset allocation. The most relevant consideration is:
Post-tax returns of each asset class
Only the pre-tax returns shown in fund factsheets
Only the asset class that gave the highest return last year
The number of securities in each asset class
Taxes reduce realised returns differently across assets and holding periods. Comparing post-tax expected returns helps choose an efficient allocation for the client.
Strategic asset allocation for a client is primarily determined by:
Next month's market outlook given by a television analyst
The asset class with the highest return over the past six months
Long-term objectives, risk profile and constraints
The portfolio manager's personal investment preferences
Strategic allocation is the long-term policy mix based on the client's profile. Short-term market views belong to tactical allocation within permitted ranges.
Goal-based investing differs from a single-portfolio approach because it:
Puts all goals into one portfolio with one common risk level
Ignores the time horizon of individual goals
Focuses only on beating a benchmark index every year
Builds separate allocations for each goal
Goal-based investing segments wealth by goals such as education, home or retirement, each with its own horizon and risk. This can make allocations and progress clearer to clients.
A client inherits ₹2 crore and has no immediate need for the money. Before investing, the portfolio manager should:
Update the client's profile and IPS
Invest the full amount immediately in the existing strategy without review
Advise the client to keep the money in a savings account permanently
Invest all of it in a single high-conviction stock
A major change in wealth can change risk capacity, goals and constraints. The manager should reassess the profile and update the IPS before deploying the new money.
During the feedback stage of portfolio management, the manager mainly:
Opens the client's demat and bank accounts for the first time
Collects KYC documents from the client
Reviews results against objectives and adjusts
Signs the PMS agreement with the client
Feedback involves measuring performance, comparing it with objectives and benchmarks, and adjusting the portfolio or IPS. Account opening and KYC happen at the start.
Which factor most increases a client's ability to take risk?
A large loan EMI due every month with uncertain income
A planned large withdrawal within the next year
Total dependence on the portfolio for daily living expenses
A long horizon with stable income
Risk capacity rises with longer horizons, stable income and lower liabilities. Heavy obligations, near-term withdrawals and dependence on the portfolio reduce capacity.

Taxation.overview: This chapter explains the taxation of investments relevant to portfolio managers and their clients: capital gains on equity, debt and mutual fund units, holding period rules, short-term and long-term rates, indexation (where applicable), set-off and carry-forward of losses, dividend and interest income, STT, GST on fees, TDS for non-residents and tax treatment of PMS expenses. Rates and rules change frequently, especially through Union Budgets and the new Income-tax Act, so focus on principles and confirm current rates.
questions: For capital gains purposes, the holding period of shares bought through PMS is counted from:
The date the client signed the PMS agreement with the manager
The start of the financial year in which the shares were bought
The date the portfolio manager obtained SEBI registration
The date the client acquired each share
Each security in the client's name has its own acquisition date, which determines whether a gain is short-term or long-term. The agreement date or financial year start is irrelevant.
When a client transfers existing shares into a PMS account (no sale), the transfer generally:
Is not a taxable sale
Triggers long-term capital gains tax on the full value
Is treated as a gift taxable in the manager's hands
Requires payment of STT at the time of transfer
Moving securities into a PMS account held in the client's own name does not change ownership, so there is no sale and no capital gain. Original cost and dates carry over.
GST on portfolio management fees is borne by:
The custodian, from its own revenue
The client, as part of fees charged
SEBI, as part of investor protection
The companies whose shares are held in the portfolio
Portfolio management is a taxable service, so GST is levied on management and performance fees and collected from the client along with the fee.
A client has a short-term capital loss from listed shares and a long-term capital gain from listed shares in the same year. The loss:
Can be set off only against salary income
Can be set off against the long-term gain
Must be carried forward and cannot be used this year
Is permanently lost if it is not used against short-term gains
Short-term capital losses can be set off against both short-term and long-term capital gains in the same year. Long-term losses, however, can only be set off against long-term gains.
A client sells shares and immediately buys them back mainly to book a loss for tax purposes. A portfolio manager should note that:
Tax and anti-avoidance rules may apply
The loss can always be claimed with no conditions whatsoever
Such trades are banned by SEBI in all circumstances
The client will automatically receive a refund of all past taxes
Tax-loss harvesting can be legitimate, but transactions mainly designed to avoid tax may be examined under tax rules. Clients should seek professional tax advice.
Interest received on corporate bonds held in a PMS account is taxed as:
Long-term capital gains at a concessional rate
Exempt income because bonds are listed
Income at the client's slab rate
Business income of the portfolio manager
Interest is taxed as income from other sources at the client's applicable slab rate, regardless of whether the bond is listed. Gains on sale of the bond are taxed separately as capital gains.
For a non-resident PMS client, which is generally the portfolio manager's responsibility in relation to capital gains?
Paying the client's tax from its own net worth
Deciding the client's country of tax residence
Claiming treaty benefits without any documents
Facilitating TDS as required by law
For NRIs, tax must be deducted at source on capital gains, and the manager or its custodian facilitates this. Treaty benefits need documents such as a tax residency certificate.
Why do portfolio managers often track 'tax lots' in client portfolios?
To decide the number of shares a company may issue
To compute gains using correct cost and dates
To set the price band for a stock on the exchange
To calculate the market capitalisation of an index
Each purchase creates a tax lot with its own cost and date. Tracking lots lets the manager compute gains accurately and choose sales that are more tax-efficient.

Regulatory, Governance and Ethical Aspec.overview: This chapter covers SEBI (Portfolio Managers) Regulations, 2020 and allied rules: registration and eligibility, net worth, code of conduct, restrictions on investments (associates, unlisted securities, derivatives, leverage), segregation of client funds and securities, conflict of interest policy, prevention of insider trading and front-running, KYC and AML obligations, grievance redressal (SCORES, ODR), inspection and penalties, and ethical standards in client dealing. Questions often test what a portfolio manager may or may not do in practical situations.
questions: A discretionary portfolio manager can invest a client's funds in unlisted securities only:
Without any limit, if the manager believes in the company
Only if the unlisted company is owned by the manager's group
Never, because unlisted securities are banned for all PMS
Up to the SEBI-specified limit, with disclosure
SEBI caps discretionary PMS investment in unlisted securities as a share of client AUM. Non-discretionary and advisory mandates may follow client instructions within norms.
Employees of a portfolio manager who learn of large client orders and trade ahead of them personally are guilty of:
Legitimate personal investment based on their own research
Portfolio rebalancing as per the client's IPS
Front-running
Tax-loss harvesting for their own benefit
Front-running exploits knowledge of pending client orders for personal gain, harming clients. SEBI treats it as a fraudulent practice punishable under the PFUTP regulations.
Under SEBI rules, can a portfolio manager borrow funds on behalf of a client to buy securities?
Yes, up to two times the client's portfolio value
Yes, if the distributor approves the borrowing
No, PMS client portfolios cannot be leveraged
Yes, but only for buying unlisted shares
SEBI prohibits portfolio managers from leveraging client portfolios for investment, protecting clients from magnified losses. Derivatives use is also restricted to permitted purposes.
A portfolio manager's conflict of interest policy should cover situations such as:
The colour scheme used in the company's office
The number of holidays given to employees
The location of the registered office
Investing client money in associate companies
Conflicts arise where the manager or associates benefit at clients' expense, such as investing in associates or allocating trades unfairly. The policy must identify, disclose and manage them.
Which of the following must a portfolio manager do under KYC and AML norms?
Skip KYC for clients investing above ₹1 crore
Verify identity and monitor for suspicious transactions
Rely only on the distributor's oral confirmation of identity
Report clients' personal details publicly on its website
Portfolio managers are reporting entities under PMLA and must carry out KYC, risk categorisation and transaction monitoring, and report suspicious transactions to FIU-IND.
A portfolio manager's marketing brochure shows only the best five years of performance. This is a problem because:
Selective performance can mislead investors
SEBI requires brochures to show only the worst years
Performance can never be shown in marketing material
Five years is always too short a period to be legal
Advertisements must be fair and not misleading. Showing cherry-picked periods hides the full record; standardised, complete performance reporting is expected.
If a portfolio manager fails to comply with SEBI regulations, SEBI can:
Only send an advisory letter with no further action possible
Transfer the manager's clients to a mutual fund automatically
Ask the clients to pay the penalty instead
Impose penalties or suspend or cancel registration
SEBI has wide powers of inspection, adjudication and enforcement, including monetary penalties, directions to clients' benefit, and suspension or cancellation of the portfolio manager's registration.
A portfolio manager receives a complaint from a client. Ideally it should:
Ignore it unless SEBI also receives the complaint
Ask the client to approach the stock exchange first
Close the client's account to avoid the complaint
Resolve it promptly and record it
Intermediaries must address complaints quickly, maintain records and report status. Unresolved complaints may be escalated by the client through SCORES and ODR.

Introduction to Indices.overview: This chapter explains what market indices are, why they matter and how they are built. It covers index uses (benchmarking, passive products, derivatives, market sentiment), construction methods (price-weighted, equal-weighted, free-float market-cap weighted, factor and smart-beta indices), base value and divisor, rebalancing and reconstitution, and the main Indian indices across equity and debt. For portfolio managers, the key focus is choosing appropriate benchmarks and understanding how index methodology affects measured performance.
questions: An index starts with a base value of 1,000. If the total free-float market value of its constituents rises 12% from the base date, the index value is:
A market-cap weighted index moves in proportion to the aggregate free-float value: 1,000 × 1.12 = 1,120. The base value simply sets the starting level.
Smart-beta or factor indices differ from traditional cap-weighted indices because they:
Always contain exactly the same stocks and weights as the Nifty 50
Weight stocks by factors such as value or quality
Are calculated only once every five years by the stock exchange
Include only government securities and no equities at all
Factor indices use rules based on characteristics like value, momentum, low volatility or quality to select or weight stocks, aiming to capture specific return drivers.
